stem: Arrows fly straight in the direction they point, over any cells, until they leave the grid. In how many empty cells can a balloon be placed so that NO arrow can hit it?
solution: Draw the path of every arrow to the edge of the grid and mark each cell it crosses. The empty cells never crossed are safe: (row 1, column 3), (row 1, column 5), (row 5, column 3), (row 5, column 5). That is 4 cells.

stem: There is a three-digit number. In this number, one even digit (not zero) occurs twice. The third digit is the sum of the digits occurring twice. What is the sum of all the digits?
solution: The repeated even digit can be 2 or 4 (6 would make a third digit 12). With 2, 2: third digit 4, digits 2, 2, 4, sum 8. With 4, 4: third digit 8, digits 4, 4, 8, sum 16.

stem: There is a three-digit number. In this number, one odd digit occurs twice. The third digit is three times the digit occurring twice. What is the sum of all the digits?
solution: The repeated odd digit can be 1 or 3 (5 would make the third digit 15). With 1, 1: third digit 3, sum 5. With 3, 3: third digit 9, sum 15.

stem: Chris bought a notebook for Rs. 150, a compass box for Rs. 30 less than the notebook, and a water bottle for Rs. 90 more than the compass box. What is the total cost of all three items?
solution: Compass box = 150 − 30 = Rs. 120. Water bottle = 120 + 90 = Rs. 210. Total = 150 + 120 + 210 = Rs. 480.

stem: Mina bought a book for Rs. 95, a pen for Rs. 15 less than the book, and a bag for Rs. more than the pen. What is the total cost of all three items?

Bhanu has some money in notes of Rs. 10, Rs. 20 or Rs. 50. Bhanu has exactly four notes and they are of only two types (denominations). Which of the following can NOT be the total amount of money Bhanu has?
solution: With four notes of exactly two types, the possible totals are 50, 60, 70, 80, 110, 120, 140, 160, 170. 100 is not in this list.

stem: Kabir has some money in notes of Rs. 5, Rs. 20 or Rs. 50. Kabir has exactly three notes and they are of only two types (denominations). Which of the following can NOT be the total amount of money Kabir has?
solution: With three notes of exactly two types, the possible totals are 30, 45, 60, 90, 105, 120. 70 is not in this list.

stem: A, B, C and D stand for different digits. In the subtraction below, what will come in place of B and D?
solution: The only digits that work are A = 8, B = 0, C = 9, D = 1: 8091 − 1908 = 6183. So B = 0 and D = 1.

stem: A, B, C and D stand for different digits. In the subtraction below, what will come in place of A and C?
solution: The only digits that work are A = 9, B = 8, C = 0, D = 2: 9802 − 2089 = 7713. So A = 9 and C = 0.

stem: Asha, Bina and Chitra are friends. Asha has Rs. 15 more than Bina, and Chitra has the same amount as Bina. They pool all their money and share it equally. After the sharing, who gets more money than she had before?
solution: Let Bina and Chitra each have x, so Asha has x + 15. The equal share is the total ÷ 3 = x + 5. Bina and Chitra each had x, and now have x + 5, so both gain. Asha loses.

stem: Raj has Rs. 30 less than Sam, and Tej has Rs. 30 more than Sam. They pool all their money and share it equally. After the sharing, who gets exactly the same amount as he had before?
solution: If Sam has x, Raj has x − 30 and Tej has x + 30. The total is 3x, so each share is x. Sam keeps exactly what he had; Raj gains 30 and Tej loses 30.

stem: When the digits of a 3-digit number are reversed, the difference between the new number and the original number is zero. The sum of the digits is more than 5. What is the minimum possible sum of the digits?
solution: Reversing gives the same number only for numbers like aba (a palindrome). The sum is 2a + b. It must be more than 5, and a ≥ 1: a = 1, b = 4 gives 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, and nothing smaller is more than 5.

stem: When the digits of a 5-digit number are reversed, the new number is the same as the original number. The sum of the digits is an odd number. What is the minimum possible sum of the digits?
solution: The number looks like abcba, so the sum is 2a + 2b + c. It is odd only if c is odd. The smallest case: a = 1, b = 0, c = 1 gives 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 = 3.

stem: A 4-digit number (digits may repeat) is chosen so that the sum of its digits is not less than 33. How many single-digit whole numbers (0 to 9) can never appear in such numbers?
solution: The largest digit sum is 9 × 4 = 36. Sums of 33 or more need every digit to be large: the smallest digit that can appear is 6 (9 + 9 + 9 + 6 = 33). Digits 0 to 5 can never appear. That is 6 digits.

stem: A 4-digit number (digits may repeat, first digit not zero) is chosen so that the sum of its digits is at most 4. How many single-digit whole numbers (0 to 9) can never appear in such numbers?
solution: With a digit sum of at most 4, no digit can be bigger than 4 (e.g. 4000). Digits 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 can appear. Digits 5 to 9 can never appear. That is 5 digits.

stem: Anita was studying when the lights went off. Anita lit two candles of equal length, but one was thicker than the other. The thick candle lasts 9 hours and the thin candle lasts 3 hours less. When Anita finally went to sleep, the thick candle was twice as long as the thin candle. For how long did Anita study by candlelight?
solution: After t hours the thick candle has (1 − t/9) of its length left and the thin candle has (1 − t/6). Setting (1 − t/9) = 2 × (1 − t/6) gives t = 4.5 hours = 4 hours 30 minutes.

stem: Bilal was studying when the lights went off. Bilal lit two candles of equal length, but one was thicker than the other. The thick candle lasts 12 hours and the thin candle lasts 4 hours less. When Bilal finally went to sleep, the thick candle was twice as long as the thin candle. For how long did Bilal study by candlelight?
solution: After t hours the thick candle has (1 − t/12) of its length left and the thin candle has (1 − t/8). Setting (1 − t/12) = 2 × (1 − t/8) gives t = 6 hours = 6 hours.

stem: Meera must work 5 straight days and rest on the next day, and this goes on in the same way. Meera started work on a Wednesday. On which day of the week will Meera take the 10th rest?
solution: One cycle has 5 work days and 1 rest day = 6 days. The 10th rest is on day 10 × 6 = 60. Counting 60 days from Wednesday (day 1), the day of the week is Saturday (because the weekday repeats every 7 days).

stem: Naveen must work 3 straight days and rest on the next day, and this goes on in the same way. Naveen started work on a Friday. On which day of the week will Naveen take the 7th rest?
solution: One cycle has 3 work days and 1 rest day = 4 days. The 7th rest is on day 7 × 4 = 28. Counting 28 days from Friday (day 1), the day of the week is Thursday (because the weekday repeats every 7 days).

stem: Tara runs in a playground. One complete round takes 4 minutes. After every 3 rounds, Tara rests for 6 minutes before running again. If Tara has just completed round number 9 at 5:50 PM, at what time did Tara start running?
solution: Running time = 9 × 4 = 36 minutes. Rests taken before round 9 finishes: after rounds 3, 6 = 2 rests × 6 = 12 minutes. Total = 48 minutes. 5:50 PM − 48 minutes = 5:02 PM.

stem: Vikram runs in a playground. One complete round takes 6 minutes. After every 2 rounds, Vikram rests for 4 minutes before running again. If Vikram has just completed round number 8 at 7:20 PM, at what time did Vikram start running?
solution: Running time = 8 × 6 = 48 minutes. Rests taken before round 8 finishes: after rounds 2, 4, 6 = 3 rests × 4 = 12 minutes. Total = 60 minutes. 7:20 PM − 60 minutes = 6:20 PM.

stem: Priya takes 25 minutes to reach the library. Rohan reaches the library 20 minutes after Priya. If Rohan reaches at 6:10 PM, at what time did Priya leave home?
solution: Priya reaches 20 minutes before Rohan: 6:10 − 0:20 = 5:50 PM. She left 25 minutes earlier: 5:50 − 0:25 = 5:25 PM.

stem: Sana takes 35 minutes to reach school. Dev reaches school 40 minutes before Sana. Dev reaches at 9:15 AM, at what time did Sana leave home?

stem: A clock shows the correct time at 8:00 AM. After this, the clock loses 10 minutes every hour. What is the actual time when the clock shows 1:00 PM?
solution: The clock moved 300 minutes on its face. In every 60 real minutes it shows 50 minutes, so real time = 300 × 60 ÷ 50 = 360 minutes after 8:00 AM, which is 2:00 PM.

stem: A clock shows the correct time at 1:00 PM. After this, the clock gains 15 minutes every hour. What is the actual time when the clock shows 7:15 PM?
solution: The clock moved 375 minutes on its face. In every 60 real minutes it shows 75 minutes, so real time = 375 × 60 ÷ 75 = 300 minutes after 1:00 PM, which is 6:00 PM.

stem: Aman, Bela and Chirag shared 90 mangoes equally among themselves. Which of the following statements can be TRUE?

stem: Dev, Eli, Fay and Gus shared 100 stickers equally among themselves. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

stem: There are three brothers: Anil, Arun and Amit. The product of their ages is 99. Anil and Arun are twins. All three are younger than 15. How old is Amit?
solution: The twins have the same age t, so t × t × age = 99. Trying ages less than 15 gives t = 3 and the third brother is 99 ÷ (3 × 3) = 11 years old.

stem: There are three brothers: Raj, Ravi and Ritu. The product of their ages is 150. Raj and Ravi are twins. All three are younger than 15. How old is Ritu?
solution: The twins have the same age t, so t × t × age = 150. Trying ages less than 15 gives t = 5 and the third brother is 150 ÷ (5 × 5) = 6 years old.

stem: Isha has 15 sweets, Jay has 13 sweets, Kiran has 19 sweets, and Lata has 21 sweets. Which two of them have a total number of sweets that can be shared equally among three people?
solution: A total can be shared equally among 3 people if it is a multiple of 3. Isha + Jay = 28; Isha + Kiran = 34; Isha + Lata = 36; Jay + Kiran = 32; Jay + Lata = 34; Kiran + Lata = 40. Only one total is a multiple of 3.

stem: Mohit has 24 sweets, Nina has 11 sweets, Om has 17 sweets, and Pia has 30 sweets. Which two of them have a total number of sweets that can be shared equally among three people?
solution: A total can be shared equally among 3 people if it is a multiple of 3. Mohit + Nina = 35; Mohit + Om = 41; Mohit + Pia = 54; Nina + Om = 28; Nina + Pia = 41; Om + Pia = 47. Only one total is a multiple of 3.

stem: A cube of side 12 cm is cut into 27 equal small cubes. What is the side length of each small cube?
solution: 27 small cubes make 3 × 3 × 3 along the three edges. So each edge of 12 cm is cut into 3 parts: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm.

stem: A cube of side 15 cm is cut into 125 equal small cubes. What is the side length of each small cube?
solution: 125 = 5 × 5 × 5, so each edge is cut into 5 parts: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 cm.

stem: An online sale for gadgets lasts for 4 hours. The whole buying process for one product takes 15 minutes. Sameer buys the maximum number of products possible. Since more products are needed, Sameer calls a friend to help, starting 1 hour before the end of the sale. The friend also takes 15 minutes for each product. What is the maximum number of products both of them can buy together?
solution: Before the friend joins: 3 hours = 180 minutes → 12 products. In the last 1 hour(s), each person buys 4 products, so together 8. Total = 12 + 8 = 20.

stem: An online sale for gadgets lasts for 5 hours. The whole buying process for one product takes 20 minutes. Tina buys the maximum number of products possible. stem: Which of the following statements is/are sufficient to answer the question? Question: P is a 3-digit number. Is P divisible by 2? Statement 1: The last digit of P is 7. Statement 2: The sum of the digits of P is 9.
options: The question cannot be answered even using both statements
solution: A number ending in 7 is odd, so it is not divisible by 2: statement 1 is enough. The digit sum 9 does not decide it (108 is even, 117 is odd), so statement 2 is not enough.

stem: Which of the following statements is/are sufficient to answer the question? Question: Q is a 3-digit number. Is Q divisible by 6? Statement 1: Q is divisible by 2. Statement 2: Q is divisible by 3.
options: The question cannot be answered even using both statements
solution: A number is divisible by 6 only when it is divisible by both 2 and 3. Statement 1 alone or statement 2 alone is not enough, but together they answer the question.

stem: A, B, C, D and E buy mangoes in each round. There are 4 rounds, and in every round: • Each person buys a different number of mangoes from 1 to 5 • A buys the least, E buys the most, and C buys more than D but less than B After 4 rounds, all the mangoes are shared equally among the five of them. Who gets the same number of mangoes as the total number he or she bought?
solution: In each round the numbers 1 to 5 are used, so the five buy A = 1×4 = 4, B = 4×4 = 16, C = 3×4 = 12, D = 2×4 = 8, E = 5×4 = 20 in all. Total = 60, so each gets 12. Only C bought exactly 12.

stem: V, W, X, Y and Z buy mangoes in each round. solution: In each round the numbers 1 to 5 are used, so the five buy V = 4×6 = 24, W = 5×6 = 30, X = 3×6 = 18, Y = 1×6 = 6, Z = 2×6 = 12 in all. Total = 90, so each gets 18. Only X bought exactly 18.

stem: Which statement is DEFINITELY true for the number described? Statement: A 5-digit number is formed using single-digit whole numbers such that the first digit is even and the other four digits are all odd.
options: The number is always a multiple of 5
The sum of the digits is always even
The sum of the digits is always 40
solution: The four odd digits add up to an even number, and an even first digit keeps the total even, so the digit sum is always even. The last digit is odd, so the number is never a multiple of 10 or of 2; it may or may not be a multiple of 5; and the largest digit sum is 8 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 44, not always 40.

stem: Which statement is DEFINITELY true for the number described? Statement: A 4-digit number is made so that its digits are odd, even, odd, even from left to right.
options: The number is always a multiple of 4
The number is always a multiple of 5
The sum of the digits is always odd
solution: The last digit is even, so the number is always even. It need not be a multiple of 4 (for example 1 2 1 2 is, but 1 2 1 4 is not), it need not end in 0 or 5, and the digit sum (odd + even + odd + even) is always even, so it is never odd.

solution: The second largest number is 95403. Placing each digit in its correct position by swapping pairs needs 3 swaps at least (count the swaps cycle by cycle).

stem: A 9-digit number X has all different digits. Using the digits of X, two 6-digit numbers and Z are formed such that no digit repeats within Y or within Z. What is the MINIMUM number of digits that Y and Z must have in common?
solution: Y and Z together use 6 + 6 = 12 digit places, but X has only 9 different digits. So at least 12 − 9 = 3 digits must be shared.

stem: A 10-digit number X has all different digits. Using the digits of X, a 6-digit number Y and a 7-digit number Z are formed such that no digit repeats within Y or within Z. What is the MINIMUM number of digits that Y and Z must have in common?
solution: Y and Z use 6 + 7 = 13 digit places, but X has only 10 different digits. So at least 13 − 10 = 3 digits must be shared.

stem: A 7-digit number has the property that the number formed by its first four digits is the same as the number formed by its last four digits (order unchanged). What is the minimum number of times any digit can appear in this number?
solution: Writing the number as p1 p2 p3 p4 p5 p6 p7 with p1p2p3p4 = p4p5p6p7 gives p1 = p4 = p7, p2 = p5, p3 = p6. So the number looks like a b c a b c a, and the digits b and c (each used twice) can be the least frequent.

stem: A 6-digit number has the property that the number formed by its first four digits is the same as the number formed by its last four digits (order unchanged). What is the minimum number of times any digit can appear in this number?
solution: With p1p2p3p4 = p3p4p5p6 we get p1 = p3 = p5 and p2 = p4 = p6. So the number looks like a b a b a b, and each digit appears at least 3 times (6 if a and b are the same).

stem: Which digit appears in the tens place of the second largest 5-digit number formed using the digits 2, 4 and 9, where each of the three digits is used at least once?
solution: The largest number is 99942 and the second largest is 99924. Its tens digit is 2.

stem: Which digit appears in the tens place of the second smallest 5-digit number formed using the digits 3, 6 and 8, where each of the three digits is used at least once?
solution: The smallest number is 33368 and the second smallest is 33386. Its tens digit is 8.

stem: A 6-digit number is formed such that all its digits are different and the sum of all the digits is 17. What is the highest digit this number can have?
solution: Six different digits add up to at least 0+1+2+3+4+5 = 15. Only 2 more can be added, so the largest digit can be at most 5 + 2 = 7 (digits 0,1,2,3,4,7).

stem: A 5-digit number is formed such that all its digits are different and the sum of all the digits is 13. What is the highest digit this number can have?
solution: Five different digits add up to at least 0+1+2+3+4 = 10. The other digits are as small as possible, so the largest digit can be at most 4 + 3 = 7.

stem: A shopkeeper has some chocolates. The first customer buys half of them and 1 more. The second customer buys half of the remaining chocolates and 1 more. The third customer buys half of what is left and 1 more. After this, 2 chocolates are left. How many chocolates were there at the beginning?
solution: Work backwards. Before each customer: (left + 1) × 2. 2 → 6 → 14 → 30. So there were 30 chocolates.

stem: A box has some oranges. Meena takes half of them and 2 more. Then Neha takes half of the remaining oranges and 2 more. Then Omi takes half of what is left and 2 more. Now 3 oranges are left in the box. How many oranges were in the box at the start?
solution: Work backwards. Before each person: (left + 2) × 2. 3 → 10 → 24 → 52. So there were 52 oranges.

stem: In a club, every member joins exactly one activity. 1/4 of the members join Dance, 1/6 join Art, 1/3 join Music and the rest join Drama. What is the least possible number of members in the club?
solution: The rest is 1 − 1/4 − 1/6 − 1/3 = 1/4. The number of members must be a multiple of 4, 6 and 3 (and of 4). The smallest such number is 12.

stem: Every student in a class chooses exactly one sport. 2/5 choose Cricket, 1/3 choose Football, 1/6 choose Chess and the rest choose Hockey. What is the least possible number of students in the class?
solution: The rest is 1 − 2/5 − 1/3 − 1/6 = 1/10. The number of students must be a multiple of 5, 3, 6 and 10. The smallest is 30.

stem: Raj owns 3/8 of a field. Rahul owns 2/5 of the remaining part. What fraction of the whole field is not owned by either of them?
solution: Remaining after Raj = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8. Rahul owns 2/5 of 5/8 = 2/8. Together they own 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8, so 3/8 is not owned.

stem: Asha plants vegetables on 1/3 of a garden. Bina plants flowers on 3/4 of the remaining part. What fraction of the whole garden is still empty?
solution: Remaining after Asha = 2/3. Bina uses 3/4 of 2/3 = 1/2. Used = 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6, so 1/6 is empty.

stem: In a row of 25 children, Anil is 9th from the left and Bela is 8th from the right. How many children stand between them?
solution: Bela is 25 − 8 + 1 = 18th from the left. Children between Anil (9th) and Bela (18th) = 18 − 9 − 1 = 8.

stem: In a queue of 30 people, Dev is 12th from the front and Esha is 11th from the back. How many people stand between them?
solution: Esha is 30 − 11 + 1 = 20th from the front. People between = 20 − 12 − 1 = 7.

stem: Three-quarters of the coins in a bag are silver. One-third of the silver coins are old. Every part is a whole number of coins. Which could be the total number of coins in the bag?
solution: The total must be a multiple of 4 (for 3/4) and the silver coins (3/4 of total) must be a multiple of 3, so the total is a multiple of 12. Only 36 works.

stem: Two-fifths of the marbles in a jar are blue. One-fourth of the blue marbles are striped. Every part is a whole number of marbles. Which could be the total number of marbles in the jar?
solution: The total must be a multiple of 5, and the blue marbles (2/5 of total) must be a multiple of 4, so the total must be a multiple of 10 that gives a multiple of 4: only 40 works (blue = 16, striped = 4).

stem: A flat round pizza is cut with 4 straight cuts. Each cut is a full straight line across the pizza. At the most, how many pieces can be made?
solution: With n straight cuts the greatest number of pieces is 1 + (1 + 2 + … + n). For 4 cuts: 1 + 10 = 11.

stem: A flat chapati is cut with 5 straight cuts. Each cut is a full straight line across it. At the most, how many pieces can be made?
solution: Each new cut can cross all earlier cuts, adding 1 more piece than the number of earlier cuts: 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 16.

stem: 6 times me is a whole and a half. Which fraction am I?
solution: A whole and a half is 3/2. Divide by 6: 3/2 ÷ 6 = 3/12 = 1/4.

stem: Three friends take cookies from a plate one after another. Each takes exactly half of the cookies on the plate at that time. After the third friend, 3 cookies are left. How many cookies were on the plate at the start?
solution: Work backwards by doubling: 3 → 6 → 12 → 24.

stem: Ravi is facing North. He makes these turns one after another: 1/4 turn clockwise, 1/4 turn clockwise, 1/4 turn anticlockwise, 1/2 turn, and then 1/4 turn clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
solution: Count clockwise quarter turns as +1, anticlockwise as −1, a half turn as 2: 1 + 1 − 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 quarter turns. Starting at North this gives North.

stem: Sonia is facing East. She turns 1/4 anticlockwise, then 1/2 turn, then 1/4 clockwise, then 1/4 anticlockwise, then 1/4 anticlockwise. Which direction is she facing now?
solution: Count clockwise quarter turns as +1 and anticlockwise as −1: −1 + 2 + 1 − 1 − 1 = 0. Starting from East, a turn of 0 quarter turns gives East.

stem: The minute hand of a clock points at 12. It turns 3/4 of a full turn clockwise and then 1/2 of a full turn anticlockwise. At which number does it point now?
solution: 3/4 clockwise = +3 quarter turns, 1/2 anticlockwise = −2 quarter turns. Net = +1 quarter turn clockwise, which moves the hand from 12 to 3.

stem: A hand of a clock points at 6. It turns 1/2 turn clockwise, then 1/4 turn clockwise, and then 3/4 turn anticlockwise. At which number does it point now?
solution: +2 + 1 − 3 = 0 quarter turns, so the hand is back at 6.

stem: Prachi is facing East. She makes these turns one after another (each is a right-angle turn): Left, Left, Right, Left, Left, Right. Which direction is she facing now?
solution: Left = −1, Right = +1. L L R L L R gives −1 −1 +1 −1 −1 +1 = −2 quarter turns, which is a half turn. From East a half turn gives West.

stem: Amit is facing South. He makes these right-angle turns one after another: Right, Right, Right, Left, Right. Which direction is he facing now?
solution: Right = +1, Left = −1. R R R L R gives +1 +1 +1 −1 +1 = +3 quarter turns. From South, 3 quarter turns clockwise gives East.

stem: The first picture is the original pattern. The other pictures show the pattern turned in some way. Which picture CANNOT be obtained by only turning (rotating) the original, without flipping it over?
solution: Turning keeps the pattern the same way round; flipping makes a mirror image. Three of the pictures are turns of the original by 1/4, 1/2 or 3/4 turn. The odd one out is the mirror image.

stem: The first picture is the original pattern. Three of the other pictures are turns of it. Which picture CANNOT be obtained by only turning the original (no flipping)?
solution: Turning keeps the pattern the same way round; flipping makes a mirror image. The picture that is a mirror image of a turned copy is the odd one out.

stem: Picture A is turned to get picture B. Which turn does this?
options: It is impossible by turning alone
solution: Turn picture A clockwise by one quarter at a time and compare with B. B matches after 1 quarter turn(s), i.e. 1/4 turn clockwise.

stem: Picture A is turned to get picture B. Which turn does this?
options: It is impossible by turning alone
solution: Turn picture A clockwise by one quarter at a time and compare with B. B matches after 3 quarter turn(s), i.e. 3/4 turn clockwise (or 1/4 turn anticlockwise).

stem: Pratik is facing West. He turns 1/2 turn anticlockwise, then 1/4 turn clockwise, then 1/2 turn clockwise. In which direction is he facing at the end?
solution: −2 + 1 + 2 = +1 quarter turn clockwise. From West, one quarter clockwise gives North.

stem: Tara is facing North. She turns 3/4 turn clockwise, then 1/2 turn anticlockwise, then 1/4 turn anticlockwise. In which direction is she facing at the end?
solution: 3 − 2 − 1 = 0 quarter turns, so she faces North again.

stem: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F sit around a round table in this order going clockwise. Now everyone moves 2 seats anticlockwise at the same time. Who now sits in the seat in which A was sitting at the start?
solution: Moving 2 seats anticlockwise, each person goes to the seat two places before theirs. The person who started two seats clockwise from A, i.e. C, now sits in A's old seat.

stem: Six children P, Q, R, S, T and U sit around a round table in this order going clockwise. Now everyone moves 4 seats clockwise at the same time. Who now sits in the seat in which S was sitting at the start?
solution: Moving 4 seats clockwise is the same as moving 2 seats anticlockwise (6 seats in all). So the person who started two seats clockwise from S, i.e. U, now sits in S's old seat.

stem: Rohan faces North and Kamini faces East. Rohan makes three 1/4 turns clockwise. Kamini makes two 1/4 turns anticlockwise. Now they are facing...
solution: Rohan: North + 3 quarter turns clockwise = West. Kamini: East − 2 quarter turns = West. They face in the same direction.

stem: Meena faces South and Naveen faces West. Meena makes one 1/4 turn clockwise. Naveen makes one 1/4 turn anticlockwise and then a half turn. Now they are facing...
solution: Meena: South + 1 = West. Naveen: West − 1 + 2 = North. They face at right angles.

stem: Each arrow is the previous arrow turned by the same amount in the same direction. Which arrow comes in place of "?"
solution: Each arrow is the previous arrow turned 1/4 turn (90°) clockwise. The 4th arrow points left (270° from up), so the next arrow points up.

stem: Each arrow is the previous arrow turned by the same amount in the same direction. Which arrow comes in place of "?"
solution: Each arrow is the previous arrow turned 1/4 turn (90°) anticlockwise. The arrows point to the upper-right, upper-left, lower-left, so the next points to the lower-right.

stem: The corner blocks of a 3×3 board are coloured as shown. In each move, every blue block jumps to the next corner in the clockwise direction (top-left → top- right → bottom-right → bottom-left → top-left). What will the board look like after 5 moves?
solution: After 4 moves every block is back where it started, so 5 moves is the same as 1 move: the blocks at the top-left and top-right move to the top-right and bottom-right.

stem: The corner blocks of a 3×3 board are coloured as shown. In each move, every blue block jumps 2 corners in the clockwise direction. What will the board look like after 3 moves?
solution: Each move shifts every block by 2 corners. After 3 moves the shift is 6 corners = 1 full lap + 2 corners. So the blocks at top-left and top-right move to bottom-right and bottom-left.

stem: Four friends A, B, C and D sit at the four sides of a square table as shown (the red arrow shows the clockwise direction). In each round, everyone moves one seat clockwise. After 7 rounds, who is sitting in the seat opposite to the seat where A sat at the start?
solution: After 4 rounds everyone is back, so 7 rounds equal 3 rounds (3 seats clockwise = 1 seat anticlockwise). The seat opposite to A's first seat is seat 3 (bottom). The person who started one seat anticlockwise from it... ends there: D.
