stem: The hour hand of a clock turns steadily. How many right angles (quarter turns) does it turn through from 3 PM to 9 AM the next day?
solution: From 3 PM to 9 AM next day is 18 hours. The hour hand makes one full turn (4 right angles) in 12 hours, so in 18 hours it turns 18 ÷ 12 = 1.5 full turns = 6 right angles.

stem: A 5-digit number has exactly 3 odd digits and 2 even digits. The sum of its digits is...
solution: Each even digit adds an even amount and does not change odd/even. Three odd digits make an odd total (odd + odd + odd = odd). So the sum of the digits is always odd.

stem: A 5-digit number has exactly 4 odd digits and 1 even digit. The sum of its digits is...
solution: Four odd digits add up to an even number, and one even digit keeps it even. So the sum of the digits is always even.

stem: In a game, 1 gold coin = 4 silver coins and 1 silver coin = 3 bronze coins. Mira has 2 gold coins and 1 silver coin. She changes all of them into bronze coins. How many bronze coins does she get?
solution: 1 gold = 4 × 3 = 12 bronze, so 2 gold = 24 bronze. 1 silver = 3 bronze. Total = 24 + 3 = 27.

stem: In a shop, 1 big token = 5 medium tokens and 1 medium token = 2 small tokens. Karan has 3 big tokens, 2 medium tokens and 4 small tokens. He changes everything into small tokens. How many small tokens does he get?
solution: 1 big = 5 × 2 = 10 small, so 3 big = 30. 2 medium = 4 small. Together with 4 small: 30 + 4 + 4 = 38.

stem: The numbers 1 to 6 can be written in the shaded boxes of a column (one number per shaded box, no number repeated). The numbers must get smaller from top to bottom. In how many ways can the 3 shaded boxes be filled?
solution: Any 3 different numbers from 1 to 6 can be written in only one decreasing order. So the answer is the number of ways to choose 3 numbers out of 6 = 20.

stem: The numbers 1 to 7 can be written in the shaded boxes of a column (one number per shaded box, no number repeated). The numbers must get smaller from top to bottom. In how many ways can the 2 shaded boxes be filled?
solution: Any 2 different numbers can be written in only one decreasing order. The number of ways = number of pairs from 7 numbers = 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21.

stem: John has 6 balls and 4 balloons. A friend offers to swap 2 balls for 3 balloons as many times as John wants (but John never swaps more balls than he has). What is the greatest number of balloons John can have after swapping?
solution: 6 balls can be swapped 3 times (2 balls each time). 3 swaps give 3 × 3 = 9 balloons. Together with his 4 balloons: 4 + 9 = 13.

stem: Leela has 9 stickers and 2 cards. A friend swaps 3 stickers for 2 cards as many times as Leela wants (never more stickers than she has). What is the greatest number of cards Leela can have after swapping?
solution: 9 stickers allow 3 swaps. 3 swaps give 3 × 2 = 6 cards. With her 2 cards: 2 + 6 = 8.

stem: Look at the number 4573. Change only the ones digit to a different digit. How many different even numbers can be made?
solution: The number is even when its ones digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. The original ones digit is 3, so none of these is the original digit. That gives 5 even numbers.

stem: Look at the number 6824. You may change exactly one digit, either the tens or the ones digit, to a different digit. How many different even numbers can be made?
solution: Changing the tens digit keeps the ones digit 4, so the number stays even: 9 new numbers. Changing the ones digit to 0, 2, 6 or 8 (not 4) gives 4 more even numbers. Total = 9 + 4 = 13.

stem: Numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 are written in the boxes A, B, C and D, one number in each box, so that the signs between the boxes are true. If D = 3, what is the number in box B?
solution: Try the possible fillings that obey the signs. With D = 3 the only filling that works is A = 1, B = 4, C = 2, D = 3. So B = 4.

stem: Numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4 are written in the boxes A, B, C and D, one number in each box, so that the signs between the boxes are true. If D = 2, what is the number in box B?
solution: Try the possible fillings that obey the signs. With D = 2 the only filling that works is A = 3, B = 1, C = 4, D = 2. So B = 1.

stem: Bob has exactly one coin each of Rs 1, Rs 2, Rs 3, Rs 8 and Rs 10. He wants to buy a candy that costs Rs 14 and must pay the exact amount using some of these coins (each coin at most once). In how many different ways can he pay?
solution: Subsets that give 14: {10, 3, 1} and {8, 3, 2, 1}. There are no others, so there are 2 ways.

stem: Chitra has exactly one coin each of Rs 1, Rs 2, Rs 4, Rs 5 and Rs 9. She wants to pay exactly Rs 12 for a toy using some of these coins (each coin at most once). In how many different ways can she pay?
solution: Subsets that give 12: {9, 2, 1} and {5, 4, 2, 1}. There are no others, so there are 2 ways.

stem: How many 3-digit even numbers can be made using only the digits 5, 0 and 9? (A digit can be used more than once.)
solution: The number is even only if its last digit is 0. The first digit can be 5 or 9 (not 0): 2 choices. The middle digit can be any of the 3 digits. So there are 2 × 3 × 1 = 6 numbers.

stem: How many 3-digit even numbers can be made using only the digits 2, 0 and 7? (A digit can be used more than once.)
solution: The last digit must be 0 or 2: 2 choices. The first digit can be 2 or 7: 2 choices. The middle digit can be any of 3 digits. So 2 × 3 × 2 = 12 numbers.

stem: A 4-digit number has only even digits and uses exactly 2 different digits. What is the smallest possible sum of its digits?
solution: Use 0 and 2: the smallest such number is 2000 (the first digit cannot be 0). Digit sum = 2 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 2.

stem: A 4-digit number has only even digits and uses exactly 2 different digits. What is the greatest possible sum of its digits?
solution: Use the two biggest even digits, 8 and 6. The sum is greatest with three 8s and one 6: 8 + 8 + 8 + 6 = 30.

stem: Sam walks 4 km north, then 3 km south, then 2 km north, and finally 5 km south. How far is he from his starting point at the end, and in which direction?
solution: North is positive and south is negative: +4 − 3 + 2 − 5 = −2. So he is 2 km south of the start.

stem: Tina walks 6 m east, then 9 m west, then 5 m east, and finally 3 m east. How far is she from her starting point at the end, and in which direction?
solution: East is positive and west is negative: +6 − 9 + 5 + 3 = +5. So she is 5 m east of the start.

label: P1
stem: The picture shows a grid of small squares with a black circle in one square. How many rectangles (of any size, squares included) drawn on the grid lines contain the black circle?
solution: A rectangle containing the circle must start at or before it and end at or after it. Choices for the top edge × bottom edge × left edge × right edge: 2 × 2 × 3 × 2 = 24.

label: P2
stem: The picture shows a 4 × 4 grid with a black circle in one square. How many rectangles (of any size, squares included) drawn on the grid lines contain the black circle?
solution: Choices: top edge 2 (rows above/including) × bottom edge 3 × left edge 2 × right edge 3 = 36.

stem: A dog is tied to a pole with an 8 m rope. Four bowls of water are placed in a straight line from the pole at distances of 5 m, 8 m, 9 m and 12 m. How many bowls can the dog reach (a bowl exactly at the end of the rope can be reached)?
solution: The dog can reach any place not more than 8 m from the pole. The bowls at 5 m and 8 m are within reach; those at 9 m and 12 m are not. So 2 bowls.

stem: A cat is tied to a post with a 6 ft rope. A bowl of milk is placed 10 ft from the post. The rope is then replaced with a longer rope so that the cat can just reach the bowl. By how many feet is the new rope longer than the old one?
solution: The cat must be able to travel 10 ft from the post, so the new rope must be 10 ft. It is 10 − 6 = 4 ft longer.

stem: In a javelin throw, Bina threw 8 m farther than Arun. Chetan threw 15 m less than Bina. Deepa threw twice as far as Chetan. Arun threw 36 m. Who finished second (the second longest throw)?
solution: Arun 36 m, Bina 44 m, Chetan 29 m, Deepa 58 m. In order: Deepa (58), Bina (44), Arun (36), Chetan (29). The second longest throw is by Bina.

stem: In a high jump contest, Sia jumped 15 cm lower than Ria. Tia jumped 25 cm higher than Sia. Uma jumped 40 cm lower than Tia. Ria jumped 120 cm. Who jumped the second lowest height?
solution: Ria 120 cm, Sia 105 cm, Tia 130 cm, Uma 90 cm. From the lowest: Uma (90), Sia (105), Ria (120), Tia (130). The second lowest is Sia.

stem: A wire of length 60 cm is cut into pieces to make as many separate squares of side cm as possible. How many squares can be made?
solution: One square needs a wire of 4 × 3 = 12 cm. 60 ÷ 12 = 5 squares.

stem: A string of length 50 cm is used to make separate triangles with all sides 4 cm. What is the greatest number of triangles that can be made?
solution: One triangle needs 3 × 4 = 12 cm. 50 ÷ 12 = 4 with 2 cm left over, so 4 triangles.

stem: A snail climbs a 10 cm wall. In each minute it climbs up 3 cm, and in the next minute it slides down 2 cm. This repeats. After how many climbing minutes (counting only the minutes it climbs up) does it first reach the top?
solution: Each pair of minutes (up 3, down 2) gives a net climb of 1 cm. After 7 such pairs it is at 7 cm. On the 8th climb it goes up 3 cm to 10 cm and reaches the top. So 8 climbing minutes.

stem: A frog climbs a 20 cm pole. In each jump cycle it goes up 5 cm and then slips down 3 cm. How many upward jumps does it need to reach the top for the first time?
solution: Each cycle gains 2 cm. After 7 cycles the frog is at 14 cm, after the 8th upward jump it is at 19 cm, slips to 16 cm, then the 9th upward jump takes it to 21 cm which is above the top. So 9 jumps.

stem: Two cyclists start at the two ends of a 90 m track at the same time and ride towards each other. One rides twice as fast as the other. How far from the start of the faster cyclist do they meet?
solution: In the same time the faster one covers twice the distance of the slower one. So the distance is split 2 : 1, which makes 60 m and 30 m. The faster cyclist has covered 60 m.

stem: Two friends start at the two ends of a 100 m path at the same time and walk towards each other. Their speeds are in the ratio 3 : 2. How far from the start of the slower walker do they meet?
solution: The distance is divided in the ratio of the speeds, 3 : 2, so the faster walker covers 60 m and the slower walker covers 40 m.

stem: A cloth of length 40 m is to be cut into pieces of 1 m each. If the cloth is cut one piece at a time from one end, what is the minimum number of cuts needed?
solution: Each cut separates one 1 m piece, but the last cut gives two pieces at once. So 40 pieces need 39 cuts.

stem: A log of 12 m is cut into pieces of 2 m each. Each cut takes 3 minutes. How many minutes are needed in all?
solution: 12 m ÷ 2 m = 6 pieces, which needs 5 cuts. 5 × 3 = 15 minutes.

stem: A hut is 40 m east of a beach and a tree is 100 m east of the same beach. Sunil stands exactly in the middle of the hut and the tree. How far east of the beach is Sunil?
solution: The distance between the hut and tree is 100 − 40 = 60 m. Half of it is 30 m. So Sunil is 40 + 30 = 70 m east of the beach.

stem: A temple is 30 m west of a river and a school is 90 m west of the same river. A boy stands exactly in the middle of the temple and the school. How far west of the river he?
solution: The distance between the temple and the school is 90 − 30 = 60 m. Half is 30 m. So the boy is 30 + 30 = 60 m west of the river.

stem: The heights of 8 trees in a row are shown (in metres). How many trees (not counting the first and last) have one neighbour taller and the other neighbour shorter than themselves?
solution: Check every tree except the two at the ends: it must be between a smaller and a bigger neighbour (rising or falling through it).

stem: The heights of 9 trees in a row are shown (in metres). How many trees (not counting the first and last) have one neighbour taller and the other neighbour shorter than themselves?
solution: Check every tree except the two at the ends: it must be between a smaller and a bigger neighbour.

stem: A lamp is 3 units taller than a cup and 2 units shorter than a vase. The cup is 5 units tall. How tall is the vase?
solution: Lamp = cup + 3 = 8 units. Vase = lamp + 2 = 10 units.

stem: A book is 4 units taller than a pencil and a box is 6 units taller than the pencil. The book is 9 units tall. How much taller is the box than the book?
solution: Pencil = 9 − 4 = 5 units. Box = 5 + 6 = 11 units. Box − book = 11 − 9 = 2 units.

stem: Village A is between 12 km and 15 km from village B (the whole-number distance, both included). Village C is between 8 km and 10 km from B. B lies on the straight road between A and C. A taxi charges Rs 8 per km. What is the least amount the taxi ride from A to C can cost?
solution: The shortest distance A to C is 12 + 8 = 20 km. The least cost is 20 × 8 = Rs 160.

stem: Village P is between 6 km and 9 km from village Q (whole-number distance, both included). Village R is between 4 km and 7 km from Q. Q lies on the straight road between P and R. A taxi charges Rs 5 per km. What is the greatest amount the taxi ride from P to R can cost?
solution: The longest distance P to R is 9 + 7 = 16 km. The greatest cost is 16 × 5 = Rs 80.

label: P1
stem: The shapes below stand for digits according to the code key. Priya's locker pattern is shown. What is the sum of the digits of her locker code?
solution: Read the code digit by digit: 74927. The digits add up to 7 + 4 + 9 + 2 + 7 = 29.

label: P2
stem: The shapes below stand for digits according to the code key. Raj's locker pattern is shown. If the code is read from left to right, what is the locker code?
solution: Replace each shape by its digit from the key, left to right: 58813.

stem: A shop has 24 groups of bricks with 25 bricks in each group. 8 bricks are taken away from each group. How many bricks are left?
solution: Each group has 25 − 8 = 17 bricks left. 24 × 17 = 408.

stem: A farm has 18 crates with 30 eggs in each crate. 7 eggs are removed from each crate. How many eggs are left?
solution: Each crate has 30 − 7 = 23 eggs left. 18 × 23 = 414.

stem: A carton can hold either 8 boxes (type A) or 10 boxes (type B). Every carton must be completely full. What is the minimum number of cartons needed to pack 76 boxes?
solution: Use as many 10-box cartons as possible: 76 = 10 × 6 + 8 × 2. That uses 2 + 6 = 8 cartons.

stem: A bag can hold either 6 mangoes or 9 mangoes. Every bag must be completely full. What is the minimum number of bags needed to pack 75 mangoes?
solution: Use as many 9-mango bags as possible: 75 = 9 × 7 + 6 × 2. That is 7 + 2 = 9 bags.

stem: 6 teams are split into 2 pools of 3. In each pool every team plays every other team in its pool twice. Then one final match is played between the pool winners. How many matches are played in all?
solution: In a pool of 3 there are 3 pairs and each pair plays twice: 3 × 2 = 6 matches. Two pools give 12 matches. Add the final: 13.

stem: 10 teams are split into 2 pools of 5. In each pool every team plays every other team its pool once. Then one final match is played between the pool winners. How many matches are played in all?
solution: In a pool of 5 there are 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 matches. Two pools give 20 matches. Add the final: 21.

stem: In an exam, each correct answer gets 4 marks and each wrong answer loses 1 mark (unattempted questions get 0). Neha attempted 38 questions and 3 of them were wrong. How many marks did she score?
solution: 38 − 3 = 35 correct answers give 35 × 4 = 140 marks. The 3 wrong answers take away 3 marks. 140 − 3 = 137.

stem: In a quiz, each correct answer gets 3 marks and each wrong answer loses 1 mark. Omar attempted 50 questions and 6 of them were wrong. How many marks did he score?
solution: 50 − 6 = 44 correct answers give 44 × 3 = 132 marks. The 6 wrong answers take away 6 marks. 132 − 6 = 126.

stem: A courier company sends goods in vans of 3 sizes. A 10 kg van costs Rs 30, a 20 kg van costs Rs 50 and a 40 kg van costs Rs 80. A load of 70 kg must be sent. What is the least total cost?
solution: Try the combinations: 40 + 20 + 10 costs 80 + 50 + 30 = Rs 160; 40 + 40 costs Rs 160; 20 × 4 costs Rs 200. The least cost is Rs 160.

stem: A truck company sends goods in vans of 3 sizes. A 10 kg van costs Rs 25, a 20 kg van costs Rs 40 and a 30 kg van costs Rs 55. A load of 55 kg must be sent. What is the least total cost?
solution: Try the combinations that carry at least 55 kg: 30 + 20 + 10 = Rs 120 for 60 kg; 30 + 30 = Rs 110 for 60 kg; 20 + 20 + 20 = Rs 120. The least cost is Rs 110.

stem: A theatre has seats in rows A to F (6 rows) and columns 1 to 5. In the picture, seats in row C and in columns 3 and 5 are empty (white). All the other seats (yellow) are taken. How many seats are taken?
solution: Taken seats are in the 5 rows other than C and in the 3 columns other than 3 and 5: 5 × 3 = 15.

stem: A hall has seats in rows A to H (8 rows) and columns 1 to 6. In the picture, seats in rows C and F and in columns 2 and 5 are empty (white). All the other seats (yellow) are taken. How many seats are taken?
solution: Taken seats are in the 6 rows other than C and F and the 4 columns other than 2 and 5: 6 × 4 = 24.

stem: The number in each square is the product of the numbers in the two circles it is next to. What is the number in circle B?
solution: A × B = 56, B × C = 72, C × A = 63. Multiply the three equations: (A × B × C)² = 56 × 72 × 63 = 254016, so A × B × C = 504. Then B = 504 ÷ 63 = 8.

stem: The number in each square is the product of the numbers in the two circles it is next to. What is the number in circle A?
Three different whole numbers, each greater than 1, have a product of 455. What is their sum?
solution: 455 = 5 × 7 × 13 (all prime). So the numbers are 5, 7 and 13. Their sum = 25.

stem: Three different whole numbers, each greater than 1, have a product of 429. What is their sum?
solution: 429 = 3 × 11 × 13 (all prime). The numbers are 3, 11 and 13. Their sum = 27.

stem: A classroom has 5 rows with 6 desks in each row. The front row is removed and then 1 desk is added to each of the remaining rows. How many desks are there now?
solution: 4 rows are left. Each has 6 + 1 = 7 desks. 4 × 7 = 28.

stem: A hall has 7 rows with 8 chairs in each row. The front row and the back row are removed and then 2 chairs are added to each of the remaining rows. How many chairs are there now?
solution: 7 − 2 = 5 rows are left. Each has 8 + 2 = 10 chairs. 5 × 10 = 50.

stem: Row D is made from Row C using the same rule for each number. If Row C has 12, what number will Row D have?
solution: Check: 4 → 9, 7 → 15, 9 → 19. The rule is "multiply by 2 and add 1" (4 × 2 + 1 = 9). For 12: 12 × 2 + 1 = 25.

stem: Row D is made from Row C using the same rule for each number. If Row C has 11, what number will Row D have?
solution: Check: 3 → 7, 5 → 13, 8 → 22. The rule is "multiply by 3 and subtract 2" (3 × 3 − 2 = 7). For 11: 11 × 3 − 2 = 31.

label: P1
stem: Six boxes each hold two shapes. Group 1 = boxes where both shapes have the same colour. Group 2 = boxes where both shapes are the same kind of shape. How many boxes belong to both groups?
solution: Check each box for the same colour and for the same kind of shape. Boxes 1, 4 and 6 have both the same colour and the same shape.

label: P2
stem: Six boxes each hold two shapes. Count the boxes in which both shapes are the same kind of shape but have different colours. How many such boxes are there?
solution: Boxes with the same kind of shape: 1, 3, 5 and 6. Of these, boxes 3 and 5 have the same colour. So the boxes with different colours are 1 and 6.

stem: A big triangle is divided into 9 small equal triangles by lines parallel to its sides, as shown. How many triangles of all sizes can you find in the figure?
solution: Small triangles: 9. Triangles made of 4 small ones: 3. The whole big triangle: 1. Total = 9 + 3 + 1 = 13.

stem: A big triangle is divided into 16 small equal triangles by lines parallel to its sides, as shown. How many triangles of all sizes can you find in the figure?
solution: Small triangles: 16. Triangles made of 4 small ones: 7. Triangles made of 9 small ones: 3. The whole big triangle: 1. Total = 16 + 7 + 3 + 1 = 27.

stem: A square is cut into 4 equal squares by one vertical and one horizontal line through the centre. What is the least number of extra straight lines needed to cut it into 8 equal parts?
solution: Draw the two diagonals of the big square. Each of the 4 squares is cut into 2 equal triangles, giving 8 equal parts with 2 extra lines.

stem: A rectangle is cut into 3 equal columns by 2 vertical lines. What is the least number extra straight lines needed to cut it into 12 equal rectangles?
solution: Each column must be cut into 4 equal parts. Three horizontal lines across the whole rectangle cut every column into 4 equal parts. So 3 extra lines.

stem: What is the least number of straight lines needed to divide a rectangle into 6 equal rectangles?
solution: Use 1 horizontal line and 2 vertical lines to make a 2 × 3 arrangement: 2 × 3 = 6. That needs 1 + 2 = 3 lines. (Five parallel lines would also work, but 3 is the least.)

stem: What is the least number of straight lines needed to divide a square into 9 equal squares?
solution: Use 2 horizontal and 2 vertical lines to make a 3 × 3 arrangement: 3 × 3 = 9. That needs 2 + 2 = 4 lines.

stem: A paper is folded in half 4 times in a row (each fold halves the folded paper). How many layers of paper are there in the folded packet?
solution: Each fold doubles the layers: 2, 4, 8, 16. After 4 folds there are 16 layers.

stem: A long strip of paper is folded in half 3 times in a row, a hole is punched through the folded packet, and then the strip is opened out. How many holes does the strip have?
solution: After 3 folds there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 layers. The punch goes through all layers, so the opened strip has 8 holes.

stem: A big cube is made from 4 × 4 × 4 small cubes. The whole top layer of 16 small cubes is removed. How many small cubes are left?
solution: The big cube has 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 small cubes. Removing the top layer takes away 16, so 64 − 16 = 48 are left.

stem: A big cube is made from 3 × 3 × 3 small cubes. The 8 corner cubes are removed. How many small cubes are left?
solution: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 small cubes. Removing the 8 corners leaves 27 − 8 = 19.

stem: A 3 × 3 board is filled with the letters A, B and C so that every row and every column has each letter exactly once. Two boxes are already filled, as shown. In how many different ways can the board be completed?
solution: The completed board is ACB / CBA / BAC (rows separated by /). Every letter is forced, so there is only 1 way.

stem: A 3 × 3 board is filled with the letters A, B and C so that every row and every column has each letter exactly once. Two boxes are already filled, as shown. In how many different ways can the board be completed?
solution: The completed board is ACB / BAC / CBA (rows separated by /). Every letter is forced, so there is only 1 way.

stem: A figure is made with matchsticks so that it has 6 equal small squares in 3 columns and 2 rows, as shown. How many matchsticks are used?
solution: Horizontal sticks: 3 per line × 3 lines = 9. Vertical sticks: 2 per line × 4 lines = 8. Total = 9 + 8 = 17.

stem: A figure is made with matchsticks so that it has 12 equal small squares in 4 columns and 3 rows, as shown. How many matchsticks are used?
solution: Horizontal sticks: 4 per line × 4 lines = 16. Vertical sticks: 3 per line × 5 lines = 15. Total = 16 + 15 = 31.

stem: The figure shows the net of a cube. When the net is folded into a cube, which letter is on the face opposite to A?
solution: In a cross-shaped net, the two faces at the ends of the row of four are opposite, and the top and bottom faces are opposite. Here A is opposite F.

stem: The figure shows the net of a cube. When the net is folded into a cube, which letter is on the face opposite to Q?
solution: Fold the net face by face. The faces that never touch each other along an edge after folding are opposite. Q is opposite T.

stem: A 4 × 5 rectangle (area 20 squares) must be filled exactly, with no gaps and no overlaps, using a set of pieces. Which set of pieces CANNOT be used because the total area is wrong?
options: 3 pieces of 6 squares and 1 piece of 3 squares
2 pieces of 8 squares and 1 piece of 4 squares
solution: The pieces must add up to exactly 20 squares. Set C has 3 × 6 + 3 = 21 squares, which is too much. The other sets add up to exactly 20.

stem: A 3 × 6 rectangle (area 18 squares) must be filled exactly, with no gaps and no overlaps, using a set of pieces. Which set of pieces CANNOT be used because the total area is wrong?
options: 4 pieces of 4 squares and 1 piece of 3 squares
3 pieces of 5 squares and 1 piece of 3 squares
solution: The pieces must add up to exactly 18 squares. Set B has 4 × 4 + 3 = 19 squares, which is too much. The other sets add up to exactly 18.

stem: A big cube is made of 27 small cubes (3 × 3 × 3). Its top face and its front face (two faces that meet at an edge) are painted red. Then the big cube is taken apart. How many small cubes have exactly one red face?
solution: Top face: 9 cubes. Front face: 9 cubes. The 3 cubes along the shared edge have 2 red faces. Cubes with exactly one red face = 9 + 9 − 3 − 3 = 12.

stem: A big cube is made of 27 small cubes (3 × 3 × 3). Its top face and its bottom face (two opposite faces) are painted red. Then the big cube is taken apart. How many small cubes have no red face?
solution: The top layer (9 cubes) and the bottom layer (9 cubes) each have a red face. The middle layer has 9 cubes with no red face.

label: P1
stem: Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F are playing. The girls are A, C and F. C and E are playing chess. All the others are playing ludo. How many boys are playing ludo?
solution: Boys = B, D, E. Ludo players = A, B, D, F. Boys playing ludo = B and D = 2.

label: P2
stem: Six children P, Q, R, S, T and U are playing. The girls are Q, R and U. P, R and T are playing chess. All the others are playing carrom. How many boys are playing chess?
solution: Boys = P, S, T. Chess players = P, R, T. Boys playing chess = P and T = 2.

label: A1
stem: There are 9 coins, one of which is lighter. Method 1: weigh two coins at a time (one against one). Method 2: divide the coins into 3 groups of 3, weigh two groups and so on. Which method guarantees finding the lighter coin in fewer weighings in the worst case?
options: Neither can find the lighter coin
Both need the same number of weighings
solution: Method 1 may need up to 4 weighings. Method 2 needs only 2 weighings: the first finds the group of 3, the second finds the coin.

label: A2
stem: There are 9 coins, one of which is lighter. You weigh two coins at a time (one against one), using a new pair each time. In the worst case, what is the greatest number of weighings you need?
solution: Make pairs: 4 pairs and 1 coin left. If the first 4 weighings balance, the lighter coin must be the 9th one. So 4 weighings at most.

label: A3
stem: There are 12 coins, one of which is lighter. You weigh two coins at a time (one against one), using a new pair each time. In the worst case, what is the greatest number of weighings you need?
solution: 12 coins make 6 pairs. If the first 5 pairs balance, the lighter coin is in the last pair, which must also be weighed. So 6 weighings at most.

label: A4
stem: There are 7 coins, one of which is lighter. You weigh two coins at a time (one against one), using a new pair each time. In the worst case, what is the greatest number of weighings you need?
solution: 7 coins make 3 pairs and 1 coin left. If all 3 weighings balance, the lighter coin is the 7th. So 3 weighings at most.

label: A5
stem: There are 9 coins. You put 4 coins on each pan and keep 1 coin aside. The pans do not balance. How many coins are still suspected (could be the lighter one)?
solution: The lighter pan holds the lighter coin. That pan has 4 coins, so 4 coins are still suspected.

label: A6
stem: There are 13 coins. You put 6 coins on each pan and keep 1 coin aside. The pans do not balance. How many coins are still suspected (could be the lighter one)?
solution: The lighter pan holds the lighter coin. That pan has 6 coins, so 6 coins are still suspected.

label: A7
stem: Among 4 coins one is lighter. You weigh 1 coin against 1 coin and keep 2 coins aside. What is the greatest number of weighings (including this one) needed to be sure of the lighter coin?
solution: If the pans do not balance you know the coin at once. If they balance, the lighter coin is one of the 2 kept aside, and one more weighing finds it. So at most 2 weighings.

label: A8
stem: Among 5 coins one is lighter. You weigh 2 coins against 2 coins and keep 1 coin aside. What is the greatest number of weighings (including this one) needed to be sure of the lighter coin?
solution: If the pans balance, the coin kept aside is the lighter one (1 weighing in all). If not, the lighter pan has 2 coins and one more weighing finds it. So at most 2 weighings.

label: A9
stem: There are 9 coins. You divide them into 3 groups of 3 and weigh 2 groups against each other. After this weighing, how many coins can be ruled out (known to be of normal weight)?
solution: After one weighing you know which group of 3 holds the lighter coin. The other 2 groups (6 coins) are ruled out.

label: A10
stem: There are 27 coins. You divide them into 3 groups of 9 and weigh 2 groups against each other. After this weighing, how many coins can be ruled out (known to be of normal weight)?
solution: After one weighing you know which group of 9 holds the lighter coin. The other 2 groups (18 coins) are ruled out.

label: A11
stem: There are 27 coins, one of which is lighter. You keep dividing the suspected coins into 3 equal groups and weighing two groups. In the worst case, how many weighings are needed?
solution: 27 → 9 → 3 → 1. Each weighing divides the suspected coins by 3, so 3 weighings are enough.

label: A12
stem: There are 81 coins, one of which is lighter. You keep dividing the suspected coins into 3 equal groups and weighing two groups. In the worst case, how many weighings are needed?
solution: 81 → 27 → 9 → 3 → 1. Each weighing divides by 3, so 4 weighings are enough.

stem: Six parcels A to F are compared on a balance: A is heavier than B, C is heavier than B is heavier than D, E is heavier than C and D is heavier than F. Which parcel is the third heaviest?
solution: Arrange from heaviest to lightest: E > C > A > B > D > F. The third heaviest is A.

stem: Six fruits P to U are compared on a balance: P is heavier than Q, R is heavier than S, is heavier than R, S is heavier than T and U is heavier than P. Which fruit is the third lightest?
solution: Arrange from heaviest to lightest: U > P > Q > R > S > T. The third lightest is R.

stem: A faulty weighing machine always shows 3 kg more than the true weight. Two bags together show 20 kg when each is weighed separately and the readings are added (one reading for each bag). What is the true total weight of the two bags?
solution: Each of the two readings is 3 kg too high, so the total reading is 6 kg too high. True total = 20 − 6 = 14 kg.

stem: A faulty weighing machine always shows 2 kg less than the true weight. Three boxes are weighed one at a time and the readings are 9 kg, 12 kg and 15 kg. What is the true total weight of the three boxes?
solution: The readings add up to 36 kg. Each of the three readings is 2 kg too low, so the true total = 36 + 3 × 2 = 42 kg.

stem: John is 5 kg heavier than Bob. Sam is 3 kg lighter than Bob. Bob and Sam together weigh 57 kg. How much does John weigh?
solution: Let Bob = x. Sam = x − 3. x + x − 3 = 57, so x = 30. John = 30 + 5 = 35 kg. Check: Sam = 27, and 30 + 27 = 57.

stem: Tina weighs 4 kg less than Uma. Vera weighs 6 kg more than Uma. Tina and Vera together weigh 72 kg. How much does Uma weigh?
solution: Let Uma = x. Tina = x − 4 and Vera = x + 6. Together: 2x + 2 = 72, so x = 35. Check: Tina = 31, Vera = 41, and 31 + 41 = 72.

stem: What is the total weight of 10 tiles? Statement 1: All the tiles have the same weight. Statement 2: 4 of the tiles together weigh 12 kg.
options: Even both statements together are not sufficient
solution: Statement 1 alone gives no weight. Statement 2 alone does not say that the other tiles weigh the same. Together: each tile weighs 3 kg, so 10 tiles weigh 30 kg.

stem: What is the total weight of 6 books? Statement 1: The books are weighed in 3 pairs and each pair weighs 800 g. Statement 2: The heaviest book weighs 500 g.
options: Even both statements together are not sufficient
solution: Statement 1 alone: 3 pairs × 800 g = 2400 g, so it is sufficient. Statement 2 gives only one book, so it cannot give the total.

stem: The weights of three boxes satisfy: A + B = 50 kg, B + C = 70 kg and A is at least 20 kg. All weights are whole numbers of kg. Which weight of C is NOT possible?
solution: A ≥ 20 means B = 50 − A ≤ 30. So C = 70 − B ≥ 40. A weight of 30 kg for C is not possible.

stem: The weights of three bags satisfy: A + B = 40 kg, B + C = 60 kg and A is at least 15 kg. All weights are whole numbers of kg. Which weight of C is NOT possible?
solution: A ≥ 15 means B = 40 − A ≤ 25. So C = 60 − B ≥ 35. A weight of 30 kg for C is not possible.

stem: 15 litres of water are poured into 5 identical buckets so that 1 litre is left unfilled in each bucket. What is the capacity of one bucket?
solution: 15 L ÷ 5 = 3 L of water in each bucket. Each bucket has 1 L unfilled, so its capacity is 3 + 1 = 4 L.

stem: 24 litres of juice are poured into 6 identical jugs so that 2 litres are left unfilled in each jug. What is the capacity of one jug?
solution: 24 L ÷ 6 = 4 L of juice in each jug. Each jug has 2 L unfilled, so its capacity is 4 + 2 = 6 L.

stem: Three bags P, Q and R weigh 54 kg together. P and Q have the same weight, and R is kg heavier than P. How much does R weigh?
solution: Let P = Q = x. Then x + x + (x + 6) = 54, so 3x = 48 and x = 16. R = 16 + 6 = 22 kg.

stem: Three sacks A, B and C weigh 40 kg together. B and C have the same weight, and A 5 kg lighter than B. How much does A weigh?
solution: Let B = C = x. Then x + x + (x − 5) = 40, so 3x = 45 and x = 15. A = 15 − 5 = 10 kg.

stem: Which one is the odd one out?
solution: Litres and millilitres measure capacity (how much liquid), while kilograms measure weight.

stem: Which one is the odd one out?
solution: Grams and kilograms measure weight, while millilitres measure capacity.

stem: Look at the series of weights: 2 kg, 5 kg, 10 kg, 17 kg, ? What comes in place of "?"
solution: The differences are 3, 5, 7, … so the next difference is 9. 17 + 9 = 26 kg. (The numbers are 1 + 1, 4 + 1, 9 + 1, 16 + 1, 25 + 1.)

stem: Look at the series of capacities: 1 L, 2 L, 4 L, 7 L, 11 L, ? What comes in place of "?"
solution: The differences are 1, 2, 3, 4, so the next difference is 5. 11 + 5 = 16 L.

stem: A train has 7 bogies. Each bogie can carry at most 60 passengers, except the green bogie which can carry at most 40 passengers. What is the greatest number of passengers the train can carry?
solution: There are 6 ordinary bogies: 6 × 60 = 360. Add the green bogie: 360 + 40 = 400.

stem: A train has 5 bogies. Each bogie can carry at most 50 passengers, except the green bogie which can carry twice as many. What is the greatest number of passengers the train can carry?
solution: There are 4 ordinary bogies: 4 × 50 = 200. The green bogie carries 100. Total = 300.

label: P1
stem: Six shops are on the two sides of a straight road, three on each side. Shops at the same position on the two sides face each other (are exactly opposite). Clues: • The Toy and Sweet shops are on opposite sides of the road. • The Books shop is exactly opposite the Bakery shop. • The Bakery and Electronics shops are on opposite sides. • The Electronics and Toy shops are on opposite sides. The other shop is Dairy. Which two shops are on the same side as the Dairy shop?
solution: Books and Bakery are on opposite sides. Electronics is opposite Bakery, so Electronics is with Books. Toy is opposite Electronics, so Toy is with Bakery. Sweet is opposite Toy, so Sweet is with Books and Electronics. That fills one side (Books, Electronics, Sweet), so the Dairy shop is on the other side with Bakery and Toy.

label: P2
stem: Six shops are on the two sides of a straight road, three on each side. Shops at the same position on the two sides face each other (are exactly opposite). Clues: • The Phone shop is exactly opposite the Fruit shop. • The Book shop is exactly opposite the Pizza shop. • The Phone and Cloth shops are on opposite sides. • The Phone and Pizza shops are on opposite sides. The other shop is Shoe. Which two shops are on the same side as the Cloth shop?
solution: Phone is opposite Fruit and Pizza, so Fruit and Pizza are on the same side. Cloth is opposite Phone, so Cloth is also on that side. That side is Fruit, Pizza and Cloth; the other side is Phone, Book and Shoe.

stem: A dance class has some students. If 4 more students join, they can all be put into teams of 8 with nobody left out. Which statement is definitely true about the original number of students?
options: It leaves remainder 4 when divided by 8
solution: The new total is a multiple of 8, so the original number is 4 less than a multiple of 8, which leaves remainder 4 when divided by 8. It need not be a multiple of 5, and it is even (not odd).

stem: A choir has some singers. If 3 more singers join, they can all stand in groups of 6 with nobody left out. Which statement is definitely true about the original number of singers?
options: It is a multiple of 3 and an odd number
solution: The new total is a multiple of 6, so the original number is 3 less than a multiple of 6. It is divisible by 3 and it is odd (6k − 3 is odd). It is not a multiple of 6 or of 4 or always even.

stem: 24 soldiers stand in a rectangle of rows and columns with the same number in every row. There must be at least 2 rows and at least 2 columns, and the number of rows must be different from the number of columns. In how many different ways (rows × columns) can they stand?
solution: The pairs (rows, columns) are (2, 12), (3, 8), (4, 6) and their reverses (12, 2), (8, 3), (6, 4). Total = 6 ways.

stem: 36 children stand in a rectangle of rows and columns with the same number in every row. There must be at least 2 rows and at least 2 columns, and the number of rows must be different from the number of columns. In how many different ways (rows × columns) can they stand?
solution: The pairs are (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9) and their reverses; (6, 6) is not allowed. Total = 6 ways.

stem: How many numbers from 101 to 200 (both included) leave a remainder of 2 when divided by 3?
solution: The first such number is 101 (101 = 3 × 33 + 2) and then every 3rd number: 101, 104, …, 200. That is (200 − 101) ÷ 3 + 1 = 34 numbers.

stem: How many numbers from 50 to 150 (both included) leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 4?
solution: The first such number is 53 and the last is 149; they go up in steps of 4: (149 − 53) ÷ 4 + 1 = 25 numbers.

stem: How many 3-digit numbers are divisible by 18 and also leave a remainder of 6 when divided by 12?
solution: Numbers divisible by 18 are 18k. 18k leaves remainder 6 on division by 12 only when k is odd. The 3-digit multiples of 18 have k from 6 to 55, and the odd values of k are 7, 9, …, 55: 25 numbers.

stem: How many 3-digit numbers are divisible by 15 and also leave a remainder of 6 when divided by 9?
solution: 15k leaves remainder 6 when divided by 9 exactly when k leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3. The 3-digit multiples of 15 have k from 7 to 66, and the values k = 7, 10, 13, …, 64 give 20 numbers.

stem: In the statement 10 @ 1 < 11, the symbol @ stands for one of +, −, × or ÷. Which operation CANNOT replace @ to make the statement true?
solution: 10 − 1 = 9, 10 × 1 = 10 and 10 ÷ 1 = 10 are all less than 11. But 10 + 1 = 11 is not less than 11. So + cannot replace @.

stem: In the statement 9 @ 3 ≤ 12, the symbol @ stands for one of +, −, × or ÷. Which operation CANNOT replace @ to make the statement true?
solution: 9 + 3 = 12, 9 − 3 = 6 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3 are all at most 12. But 9 × 3 = 27 is more than 12. So × cannot replace @.

stem: Six letters stand in the order A, B, C, D, E, F. Their values are: A = 2 + 5, B = 3 × 2, C = 10 − 1, D = 4 × 3, E = 6 + 8, F = 20 − 3. If the letters are re-arranged in increasing order of value (smallest first), how many letters stay in the same position as before?
solution: Values: A 7, B 6, C 9, D 12, E 14, F 17. Sorted order: B, A, C, D, E, F. Letters in the same place: C, D, E, F (positions 3 to 6) = 4 letters.

stem: Six letters stand in the order P, Q, R, S, T, U. Their values are: P = 5 × 3, Q = 4 + 7, R = 2 × 6, S = 20 − 4, T = 9 + 8, U = 3 × 8. If the letters are re-arranged in increasing order of value (smallest first), how many letters stay in the same position as before?
solution: Values: P 15, Q 11, R 12, S 16, T 17, U 24. Sorted: Q, R, P, S, T, U. The letters S, T and U are in the same positions (4th, 5th and 6th) as before = 3 letters.

stem: A troop of 1234 soldiers stands in rows of 25. After forming as many full rows as possible, how many soldiers are left over?
solution: 25 × 49 = 1225. 1234 − 1225 = 9 soldiers are left over.

stem: A band has 1000 members. After 17 members leave, the rest stand in rows of 12. After forming as many full rows as possible, how many members are left over?
A family eats 2 slices of pizza every day for 15 days. Each pizza has 8 slices. What the least number of pizzas they must buy?
solution: 2 × 15 = 30 slices are needed. 30 ÷ 8 = 3 with remainder 6, so 4 pizzas are needed.

stem: A hostel serves 3 pieces of cake every day for 20 days. Each box has 7 pieces. What is the least number of boxes that must be bought?
solution: 3 × 20 = 60 pieces are needed. 60 ÷ 7 = 8 with remainder 4, so 9 boxes are needed.

stem: The digits 7, 4, 6, 3 are written in this order. Put + or × between each pair of neighbours. The × sign may be used only between two even digits. What is the greatest value you can get?
solution: Only 4 and 6 are both even and next to each other. 7 + 4 × 6 + 3 = 7 + 24 + 3 = 34. Using all + gives only 20.

stem: The digits 2, 8, 5, 6, 4 are written in this order. Put + or × between each pair of neighbours. The × sign may be used only between two even digits. What is the greatest value you can get?
solution: The even neighbours are (2, 8) and (6, 4). 2 × 8 + 5 + 6 × 4 = 16 + 5 + 24 = 45.

stem: Look at the series: 5, 10, 8, 16, 14, 28, ? What comes in place of "?"
solution: The pattern is: × 2, then − 2, then × 2, then − 2, … The last number is 28, and the next step is − 2. So ? = 28 − 2 = 26.

stem: Look at the series: 7, 21, 18, 54, 51, ? What comes in place of "?"
solution: The pattern is: × 3, then − 3, then × 3, then − 3, … The last number is 51, and the next step is × 3. So ? = 51 × 3 = 153.

label: P1
stem: Look at these words: TON, SIT, FIRE, BONE, MINE, TWA, BOY, SAVEN. In how many of them can you change exactly one letter (keeping the same number of letters) to make the name of a number from ZERO to TEN?
solution: Check each word: TON → TEN; SIT → SIX; FIRE → FIVE; MINE → NINE; TWA → TWO; SAVEN → SEVEN. The other words need more than one change.

label: P2
stem: Look at these words: FIVA, SEX, WHO, NIME, TEA, EIGHY, FOUL, TREE. In how many of them can you change exactly one letter (keeping the same number of letters) to make the name of a number from ZERO to TEN?
solution: Check each word: FIVA → FIVE; SEX → SIX; NIME → NINE; TEA → TEN; EIGHY → EIGHT; FOUL → FOUR. The other words need more than one change.

stem: Which of these capital letters looks the same when it is reflected in a vertical mirror line drawn through its middle?
solution: M is the same on its left and right sides. E has a horizontal mirror line (top and bottom match), and K and R have no vertical mirror line.

stem: Which of these capital letters has both a vertical and a horizontal line of symmetry?
solution: H is the same left-right and top-bottom. A has only a vertical line, E has only a horizontal line and F has none.

stem: How many lines of symmetry does this regular pentagon (5 equal sides) have?
solution: Each line of symmetry joins a corner to the middle of the opposite side. A regular pentagon has 5 corners, so 5 lines of symmetry.

stem: How many lines of symmetry does this rhombus (4 equal sides, not a square) have?
solution: The two diagonals of a rhombus are its lines of symmetry. So there are 2.

stem: A rectangular paper is folded exactly in half once. Which of these papers becomes a square after the fold?
solution: Folding halves the longer side. 8 cm by 4 cm becomes 4 cm by 4 cm, a square. 6 by 4 gives 3 by 4 or 6 by 2; 9 by 6 gives 4.5 by 6; 10 by 6 gives 5 by 6.

stem: A rectangular cloth is folded exactly in half once. Which of these cloths becomes a square after the fold?
solution: Folding halves the longer side. 14 by 7 becomes 7 by 7, a square. The other cloths do not become squares when halved.

stem: A square paper is folded in half along the middle (fold line shown by the thick edge) and the picture shows the folded paper with some squares cut out (black). When the paper is opened out again, what does it look like?
solution: The fold is on the right edge of the folded paper. Each cut square also appears at its mirror position on the other side of the fold line. The correct picture is symmetrical about the vertical middle line.

stem: A square paper is folded in half along the middle (fold line shown by the thick edge) and the picture shows the folded paper with some squares cut out (black). When the paper is opened out again, what does it look like?
solution: The fold is on the bottom edge of the folded paper. Each cut square also appears at its mirror position below the fold line. The correct picture is symmetrical about the horizontal middle line.

stem: In how many different ways can a square sheet of paper be folded along a straight line so that the two halves match exactly?
solution: The folds are along the 2 lines through the middles of opposite sides and along the 2 diagonals. That makes 4 ways.

stem: In how many different ways can a regular hexagon be folded along a straight line so that the two halves match exactly?
solution: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry: 3 through opposite corners and 3 through the middles of opposite sides.

stem: A flat shape (a polygon) is cut into two pieces by one straight line. Each piece has 5 sides. Which of these could be the number of sides of the original shape?
solution: A straight cut adds 2, 3 or 4 to the total number of sides (it adds 4 when it goes through two sides). The two pieces together have 5 + 5 = 10 sides, so the original has 10 − 4 = 6, 10 − 3 = 7 or 10 − 2 = 8 sides. Only 6 is in the list.

stem: A flat shape (a polygon) is cut into two pieces by one straight line. One piece has 3 sides and the other has 4 sides. Which of these could be the number of sides of the original shape?
solution: A straight cut adds 2, 3 or 4 to the total number of sides. The pieces together have 3 + 4 = 7 sides, so the original has 7 − 4 = 3, 7 − 3 = 4 or 7 − 2 = 5 sides. Only 5 is in the list.

stem: Picture P is reflected in the vertical line AB (placed to its right). The new picture is then reflected in the horizontal line CD (placed below it). What does the final picture look like? AB
solution: Reflecting in a vertical line flips left and right. Reflecting in a horizontal line then flips up and down. Both together turn the picture by a half turn (180°).

stem: Picture P is reflected in the vertical line AB (to its right). The new picture is then reflected in the vertical line CD (further to the right). What does the final picture look like? AB CD
solution: Reflecting in a vertical line flips left and right. Doing it twice flips back, so the final picture looks the same as P (just moved to the right).

stem: Which pair of lowercase letters look like mirror images of each other when a vertical mirror is placed between them?
solution: A vertical mirror flips left and right. The letter b flipped left-right looks like d. The pairs b/p, u/n and m/w are turned upside down (flipped top-bottom), not left-right.

stem: Which pair of lowercase letters look like mirror images of each other when a horizontal mirror is placed below the first letter?
solution: A horizontal mirror flips top and bottom. The letter b flipped top-bottom looks like p. The pairs b/d and p/q are left- right mirror images, and d/p is a half-turn.

stem: A square paper is folded in half twice: first left to right and then top to bottom. The folded paper (red edges are the folds) has one hole punched as shown. Which picture shows the paper when it is fully opened?
solution: The hole goes through 4 layers, so there are 4 holes after opening: the original and its mirror images across the vertical middle line and across the horizontal middle line.

stem: A square paper is folded in half twice: first left to right and then top to bottom. The folded paper (red edges are the folds) has one hole punched as shown. Which picture shows the paper when it is fully opened?
solution: The hole goes through 4 layers, so there are 4 holes after opening: the original and its mirror images across the vertical middle line and across the horizontal middle line.

stem: A sheet of paper is folded in half 3 times, and then 2 holes are punched through the folded packet at different places. How many holes will the sheet have when it is opened out?
solution: After 3 folds there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 layers. Each punch makes 8 holes when opened. Two punches make 2 × 8 = 16 holes.

stem: A sheet of paper is folded in half 2 times, and then 3 holes are punched through the folded packet at different places. How many holes will the sheet have when it is opened out?
solution: After 2 folds there are 2 × 2 = 4 layers. Each punch makes 4 holes when opened. Three punches make 3 × 4 = 12 holes.

label: P1
stem: A building has 10 floors. Two lifts (orange and blue) move at one floor per second. At the start the orange lift is at floor 3 going up and the blue lift is at floor 9 going up. A lift turns around at once when it reaches floor 10 or floor 1. At which floor do the two lifts meet for the first time?
solution: Orange: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 … Blue: 9, 10, 9, 8, 7 … After 4 seconds both are at floor 7.

label: P2
stem: A building has 10 floors. Two lifts (orange and blue) move at one floor per second. At the start the orange lift is at floor 4 going down and the blue lift is at floor 8 going down. A lift turns around at once when it reaches floor 10 or floor 1. At which floor do the two lifts meet for the first time?
solution: Orange: 4, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3 … Blue: 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3 … After 5 seconds both are at floor 3.

stem: A regular hexagon is cut along a line joining two opposite corners. What fraction of the hexagon's area is each of the two pieces?
solution: A line joining opposite corners is a line of symmetry, so it cuts the hexagon into two equal halves. Each piece is 1/2 of the area.

stem: A regular hexagon is cut along a line joining two corners that have exactly one corner between them (this cuts off a small triangle). What fraction of the hexagon's area is the small triangle?
solution: A regular hexagon can be divided into 6 equal triangles from its centre. The cut-off triangle has the same area as 1 of these (it is a triangle with sides s, s and 120° between), so it is 1/6 of the hexagon.

stem: A square of side 8 cm is cut into two equal rectangles by a straight line through the middle of two opposite sides. What is the perimeter of one rectangle?
solution: Each rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm. Perimeter = 2 × (8 + 4) = 24 cm.

stem: A rectangle 12 cm by 6 cm is cut into two equal squares by a straight line. What is the perimeter of one square?
solution: Each square has side 6 cm. Perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24 cm.

stem: Each small square of the grid has an area of 1 square unit. The orange shape is made of whole squares and half squares (triangles cut along a diagonal). What is the area the orange shape?
solution: Whole squares = 12. Half squares = 12, which make 6 squares. Area = 12 + 6 = 18 square units.

stem: Each small square of the grid has an area of 1 square unit. The orange shape is made of whole squares and half squares (triangles cut along a diagonal). What is the area the orange shape?
solution: Whole squares = 11. Half squares = 8, which make 4 squares. Area = 11 + 4 = 15 square units.

stem: Which of these 4 × 4 grids has exactly half of its small squares black (and the other half white)?
solution: A 4 × 4 grid has 16 small squares, so half is 8. Count the black squares in each grid: only one has exactly 8 black squares.

stem: Which of these 4 × 4 grids has exactly one quarter of its small squares black?
solution: A 4 × 4 grid has 16 small squares, so one quarter is 4. Count the black squares in each grid: only one has exactly 4 black squares.

stem: A box has length 8 cm, breadth 6 cm and height 4 cm. The length and breadth are both halved and the height is kept the same. What fraction of the original volume is the new volume?
solution: Volume = length × breadth × height. Halving two of the three measurements multiplies the volume by 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

stem: A box has length 8 cm, breadth 6 cm and height 4 cm. The length and breadth are both halved and the height is kept the same. How many of the 6 faces of the new box have exactly one quarter of the area of the matching face of the original box?
solution: The top and bottom faces (length × breadth) become 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 of the original. The four side faces each have only one measurement halved, so they become 1/2. So 2 faces.

stem: A blue rectangle (3 rows and 5 columns of unit squares) is joined with the orange piece A (2 unit squares) along its right side, as shown. How does the perimeter of the whole shape change after piece A is added? (Each small square has side 1 unit.)
solution: Perimeter before = 16 units. After adding piece A the perimeter is 18 units. So it increases by 2 units.

stem:
The blue shape is a 3 × 3 square with its top-right corner square missing. The orange piece A (1 unit square) is placed in the missing corner, as shown. How does the perimeter of the whole shape change after piece A is added? (Each small square has side 1 unit.)
- A
solution: Perimeter before = 12 units. After adding piece A the perimeter is 12 units. So it stays the same.

stem: The diameter of a circle is equal to the side of a square, both 10 cm. Take π = 3. How much greater is the area of the square than the area of the circle?
solution: Square area = 10 × 10 = 100 sq cm. Circle radius = 5 cm, so its area = 3 × 5 × 5 = 75 sq cm. Difference = 100 − 75 = 25 sq cm.

stem: The diameter of a circle is equal to the side of a square, both 8 cm. Take π = 3. How much greater is the area of the square than the area of the circle?
solution: Square area = 8 × 8 = 64 sq cm. Circle radius = 4 cm, so its area = 3 × 4 × 4 = 48 sq cm. Difference = 64 − 48 = 16 sq cm.

stem: A field is shaped like an isosceles triangle (two equal sides). Two of its sides measure 12 m and 30 m. What is the perimeter of the field?
solution: The equal sides cannot be 12 m (12 + 12 = 24 is less than 30, so the triangle would not close). So the equal sides are 30 m and 30 m, and the perimeter = 30 + 30 + 12 = 72 m.

stem: A garden is shaped like an isosceles triangle (two equal sides). Two of its sides measure 9 m and 20 m. What is the perimeter of the garden?
solution: The equal sides cannot be 9 m (9 + 9 = 18 is less than 20, so the triangle would not close). So the equal sides are 20 m and 20 m, and the perimeter = 20 + 20 + 9 = 49 m.

stem: A 6 × 6 square floor is covered with unit tiles. The tiles along the outer border are red and all the other tiles are yellow. How many yellow tiles are there?
solution: The inside is a 4 × 4 square of tiles (the border takes one tile on every side). 4 × 4 = 16 yellow tiles. (Red tiles = 36 − 16 = 20.)

stem: An 8 × 8 square floor is covered with unit tiles. The tiles in the outer two rows and columns on every side (a border 2 tiles wide) are red and all the other tiles are yellow. How many red tiles are there?
solution: The yellow part is a 4 × 4 square (8 − 2 − 2 = 4), which has 16 tiles. Red tiles = 64 − 16 = 48.

stem: Two identical regular pentagons with sides of 4 cm are joined so that they share one full side. What is the perimeter of the joined shape?
solution: Each pentagon has a perimeter of 5 × 4 = 20 cm. The shared side (4 cm) is hidden on both pentagons: 20 + 20 − 4 − 4 = 32 cm.

stem: Two identical regular hexagons with sides of 3 cm are joined so that they share one full side. What is the perimeter of the joined shape?
solution: Each hexagon has a perimeter of 6 × 3 = 18 cm. The shared side (3 cm) is hidden on both hexagons: 18 + 18 − 3 − 3 = 30 cm.

Clues: • There is exactly 1 book between the Geography and Science books • The Science book is somewhere above the English book • There are exactly 2 books between the Geography and History books • The History book is at the very top Which two books are at the top of the stack (the two highest)?
solution: Use the clues to place the books from top to bottom step by step. The only possible top two are History and Science.

Clues: • The History book is somewhere above the English book • The French book is at the very top • There is exactly 1 book between the French and English books • The French book is somewhere above the Science book Which two books are at the top of the stack (the two highest)?
solution: Use the clues to place the books from top to bottom step by step. The only possible top two are French and History.

stem: A cricket match starts at 10:15 AM and lasts 1 hour 15 minutes. After the match there is a 45-minute lunch break. At what time does the lunch break end?
solution: The match ends at 10:15 + 1:15 = 11:30 AM. The lunch break then ends at 11:30 + 0:45 = 12:15 PM.

stem: A play starts at 2:40 PM and lasts 1 hour 40 minutes. After the play, the audience has a 25-minute snack break. At what time does the snack break end?
solution: The play ends at 2:40 + 1:40 = 4:20 PM. The snack break ends at 4:20 + 0:25 = 4:45 PM.

stem: A bulb is ON for 7 minutes and then OFF for 7 minutes, again and again. It first turns on at 6:00 PM. At what time does it turn ON for the 4th time?
solution: One full ON–OFF cycle is 14 minutes. The bulb turns on for the 4th time after 3 full cycles = 42 minutes, at 6:42 PM.

stem: A lamp is ON for 5 minutes and then OFF for 3 minutes, again and again. It first turns on at 7:30 AM. At what time does it turn ON for the 5th time?
solution: One full cycle is 5 + 3 = 8 minutes. The lamp turns on for the 5th time after 4 full cycles = 32 minutes, at 8:02 AM.

stem: Look at the series of times: 9:10, 9:35, 10:00, 10:25, ? Which time comes in place of "?"
solution: Each time is 25 minutes after the one before. 10:25 + 0:25 = 10:50.

stem: Look at the series of times: 2:45, 3:20, 3:55, ?, 5:05 Which time comes in place of "?"
solution: Each time is 35 minutes after the one before. 3:55 + 0:35 = 4:30 (and 4:30 + 0:35 = 5:05 checks).

stem: An alarm rings every 3 hours, starting at 8 AM. How many times does it ring between 8 AM and 4 PM (both times included)?
solution: It rings at 8 AM, 11 AM and 2 PM. The next ring would be at 5 PM, which is after 4 PM. So 3 times.

stem: A bell rings every 2 hours, starting at 9 AM. How many times does it ring between 9 AM and 5 PM (both times included)?
solution: It rings at 9 AM, 11 AM, 1 PM, 3 PM and 5 PM. So 5 times.

stem: Four friends arrive at a party. A arrives at 5:10 PM. B arrives 20 minutes after A. C arrives 15 minutes before B. D arrives 35 minutes after C. Who arrives last?
solution: A = 5:10, B = 5:30, C = 5:15, D = 5:50. The last to arrive is D.

Four friends write at a steady speed: Raj writes 2 pages in 10 minutes, Sia writes 3 pages in 18 minutes, Tom writes 5 pages in 20 minutes and Uma writes 4 pages in 24 minutes. Who will write the most pages in 1 hour?
solution: Pages in 1 hour: Raj 12, Sia 10, Tom 15, Uma 10. Tom writes the most.

stem: Four friends colour at a steady speed: Ann colours 3 pictures in 12 minutes, Ben colours 5 pictures in 30 minutes, Cy colours 7 pictures in 28 minutes and Dee colours 2 pictures in 6 minutes. Who will colour the most pictures in 1 hour?
solution: Pictures in 1 hour: Ann 15, Ben 10, Cy 15, Dee 20. Dee colours the most.

stem: Anil and Bina run along a path of 12 boxes. Anil takes 5 seconds per box and Bina takes 4 seconds per box. Anil starts first and Bina starts 6 seconds later. Who finishes first and by how many seconds?
solution: Anil takes 12 × 5 = 60 seconds. Bina takes 12 × 4 = 48 seconds, plus 6 seconds of waiting = 54 seconds. Bina finishes 60 − 54 = 6 seconds earlier.

stem: Raj and Sam run along a path of 10 boxes. Raj takes 6 seconds per box and Sam takes 5 seconds per box. Raj starts first and Sam starts 10 seconds later. Who finishes first and by how many seconds?
solution: Raj takes 10 × 6 = 60 seconds. Sam takes 10 × 5 = 50 seconds plus 10 seconds of waiting = 60 seconds. They finish at the same time.

stem: A badminton game begins at 6:30 PM. Meena must reach the court 20 minutes before the game. She needs 5 minutes to walk to the car and then a 35-minute drive. What is the latest time she can leave home?
solution: Work backwards from 6:30 PM: 20 minutes early = 6:10 PM; minus the 35-minute drive = 5:35 PM; minus the 5- minute walk = 5:30 PM.

stem: A school concert begins at 9:00 AM. Ravi must be in his seat 15 minutes before it begins. He needs a 10-minute walk to the bus stop and then a 40-minute bus ride. What is the latest time he can leave home?
solution: Work backwards from 9:00 AM: 15 minutes early = 8:45 AM; minus the 40-minute ride = 8:05 AM; minus the 10- minute walk = 7:55 AM.

stem: Boxes in a row are painted Red, Green, Blue, Yellow again and again (box 1 is Red). A rabbit starts on box 1 and in each jump moves 3 boxes forward. What colour is the box it lands on after its 13th jump?
solution: After 13 jumps the rabbit is on box 1 + 13 × 3 = 40. The colours repeat every 4 boxes, and 40 is a multiple of 4, so it lands on the 4th colour in the pattern: Yellow.

stem: Boxes in a row are painted Red, Green, Blue, Yellow, Pink again and again (box 1 is Red). A rabbit starts on box 1 and in each jump moves 2 boxes forward. What colour is the box it lands on after its 17th jump?
solution: After 17 jumps the rabbit is on box 1 + 17 × 2 = 35. The colours repeat every 5 boxes, and 35 is a multiple of 5, so it lands on the 5th colour in the pattern: Pink.

stem: Two trains leave a station at 6:00 AM together. Train A leaves again every 15 minutes and Train B leaves again every 20 minutes. At what time do they next leave together?
solution: The trains leave together after a time that is a multiple of both 15 and 20. The smallest is 60 minutes, so they next leave together at 7:00 AM.

stem: Two buses leave a stop at 8:00 AM together. Bus P leaves again every 12 minutes and Bus Q leaves again every 18 minutes. At what time do they next leave together?
solution: The buses leave together after a time that is a multiple of both 12 and 18. The smallest is 36 minutes, so they next leave together at 8:36 AM.

stem: A two-digit number has its ones digit equal to twice its tens digit (for example 12, 24, ...). By which of these numbers is such a number always divisible?
solution: The numbers are 12, 24, 36 and 48. Each is 12 × (the tens digit), so every such number is divisible by 12. Only 12 works for all of them (36 is not divisible by 5, 7 is not a factor of 24, 9 does not divide 12).

stem: A two-digit number has its ones digit equal to three times its tens digit (for example 13, 26, ...). By which of these numbers is such a number always divisible?
solution: The numbers are 13, 26 and 39. Each is 13 × (the tens digit), so every such number is divisible by 13. They are not all divisible by 26 (13 and 39 are not).

stem: A shop has 36 chocolates and 48 toys. They are packed into identical gift boxes, each box having the same number of chocolates and the same number of toys, with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of boxes that can be made?
solution: The number of boxes must divide both 36 and 48. The greatest common factor of 36 and 48 is 12. So 12 boxes (3 chocolates and 4 toys in each).

stem: A teacher has 45 pens and 60 pencils. She packs them into identical kits, each kit having the same number of pens and the same number of pencils, with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of kits that can be made?
solution: The number of kits must divide both 45 and 60. The greatest common factor of 45 and 60 is 15. So 15 kits (3 pens and 4 pencils in each).

stem: Sam has 22 pencils and Mary has 14 pencils. They put all their pencils together and share them equally among 4 students. How many pencils does each student get?
solution: 22 + 14 = 36 pencils. 36 ÷ 4 = 9 pencils for each student.

stem: Sam has 22 pencils and Mary has 14 pencils. They put all their pencils together and share them equally among 5 students, giving each student as many as possible. How many pencils are left over?
solution: 22 + 14 = 36 pencils. 36 ÷ 5 = 7 with remainder 1, so 1 pencil is left over.

stem: There are four boxes. Box A accepts numbers that are multiples of 5, Box B accepts multiples of 3, Box C accepts even numbers and Box D accepts multiples of 4. A number card goes into every box that accepts it. Which number card goes into exactly 3 boxes?
solution: 24 is a multiple of 3 (Box B), even (Box C) and a multiple of 4 (Box D): 3 boxes. 45 and 15 go into A and B only; 3 goes into B only.

stem: There are four boxes. Box A accepts numbers that are multiples of 5, Box B accepts multiples of 3, Box C accepts even numbers and Box D accepts multiples of 4. A number card goes into every box that accepts it. Which number card goes into exactly 1 box?
solution: 3 is a multiple of 3 only, so it goes into Box B only. 15 goes into A and B, 24 into B, C and D, and 60 into all four boxes.

stem: Tiles are numbered 1, 2, 3, … along a path. A rabbit starts before tile 1 (at tile 0) and lands on every 3rd tile (3, 6, 9, …). Each jump takes 2 minutes. How many minutes does it take to land on tile 30?
solution: It lands on tiles 3, 6, …, 30, which is 30 ÷ 3 = 10 jumps. 10 × 2 = 20 minutes.

stem: Stones are numbered 1, 2, 3, … across a stream. A frog starts at stone 0 and lands on every 4th stone (4, 8, 12, …). Each jump takes 3 minutes. How many minutes does it take to land on stone 36?
solution: It lands on stones 4, 8, …, 36, which is 36 ÷ 4 = 9 jumps. 9 × 3 = 27 minutes.

stem: Four pairs of numbers are given. Three of them follow the same rule. Which pair is the odd one out?
solution: In (4, 12), (5, 15) and (6, 18) the second number is 3 times the first. In (7, 20), 3 × 7 = 21, not 20.

stem: Four pairs of numbers are given. Three of them follow the same rule. Which pair is the odd one out?
solution: In (3, 9), (4, 16) and (5, 25) the second number is the first multiplied by itself (3 × 3, 4 × 4, 5 × 5). In (6, 18) it is not (6 × 6 = 36).

stem: Two pieces of yarn are 56 cm and 98 cm long. Both are cut into pieces of the same length with nothing left over. What is the greatest possible length of each piece?
solution: The length must be a common factor of 56 and 98. The greatest common factor of 56 and 98 is 14. So 14 cm.

stem: Two ropes are 72 cm and 108 cm long. Both are cut into pieces of the same length with nothing left over. What is the greatest possible length of each piece?
solution: The length must be a common factor of 72 and 108. The greatest common factor is 36. So 36 cm.

stem: Look at the series of shapes. Each shape is a regular polygon. Which shape comes in place of "?"
solution: The shapes have 3, 4, 5, 6 sides, so each shape has one more side than the one before. The next has 7 sides.

stem: Look at the series of shapes. Each shape is a regular polygon. Which shape comes in place of "?"
solution: The shapes have 9, 7, 5 sides, so each shape has two fewer sides than the one before. The next has 3 sides.

stem: A, B and C are whole numbers. Is at least one of them divisible by 3?
options: Even both statements together are not sufficient
solution: Statement 1 alone is not enough (1 + 1 + 1 = 3, yet none of them is divisible by 3). Statement 2 alone is enough: among any three consecutive numbers exactly one is divisible by 3.

stem: P and Q are whole numbers. Is at least one of them even? Statement 1: P + Q is odd. Statement 2: P and Q are the same number.
options: Even both statements together are not sufficient
solution: Statement 1 alone is enough: an odd sum is odd + even, so exactly one of them is even. Statement 2 alone is not enough: for example P = Q = 3 has no even number.

stem: The number X has exactly two factors and the sum of its factors is 42. What is X?
solution: A number with exactly two factors has only 1 and itself as factors, so 1 + X = 42 and X = 41 (41 is prime).

stem: The number Y has exactly two factors and the sum of its factors is 24. What is Y?
solution: A number with exactly two factors has only 1 and itself as factors, so 1 + Y = 24 and Y = 23 (23 is prime).

stem: Aman starts at the origin (0, 0) of a map and can only move East or North (one step at a time, along the grid lines). The first number of a point shows how far East it is (negative means West) and the second shows how far North (negative means South). Which of these points can he reach?
solution: Moving only East and North, both numbers can only grow (never go below 0). So Aman can reach a point only if both numbers are 0 or more. Only (4, 5) fits.

stem: Diya starts at the origin (0, 0) of a map and can only move West or South (one step at a time, along the grid lines). The first number of a point shows how far East it is (negative means West) and the second shows how far North (negative means South). Which of these points can she reach?
solution: Moving only West and South, both numbers can only go down (never above 0). So Diya can reach a point only if both numbers are 0 or less. Only (−1, −4) fits.

stem: Village P is 4 km East of village Q. Village R is 3 km North of P. Village S is 6 km West of R. Village T is 5 km South of S. In which direction is T from Q?
solution: Put Q at (0, 0). P = (4, 0), R = (4, 3), S = (−2, 3), T = (−2, −2). T is 2 km West and 2 km South of Q, so it is to the South- West.

stem: Village B is 5 km North of village A. Village C is 3 km West of B. Village D is 3 km South of C. Village E is 7 km East of D. In which direction is E from A?
solution: Put A at (0, 0). B = (0, 5), C = (−3, 5), D = (−3, 2), E = (4, 2). E is 4 km East and 2 km North of A, so it is to the North- East.

stem: A signpost at a crossing has four arms labelled N, E, S, W. After a storm the whole signpost has been turned, and the arm labelled E now points to the South-West. In which direction does the arm labelled N now point?
solution: E to South-West is a turn of 135° clockwise (East → South → South-West = 90° + 45°). Turn the N arm by the same 135°: North → East → South-East.

stem: A signpost at a crossing has four arms labelled N, E, S, W. After a storm the whole signpost has been turned, and the arm labelled S now points to the North-East. In which direction does the arm labelled W now point?
solution: S (180°) to North-East (45°) is a turn of 225° clockwise. Turn the W arm (270°) by 225°: 270° + 225° = 135°, which is South-East.

stem: The picture shows the path of a boy who starts at S and walks along the arrows. How many right turns (clockwise quarter turns) does he make along the whole path?
solution: The directions are N → N → E → E → S → E → E → N → N → W. Each right turn is N→E, E→S, S→W or W→N. There are 2 right turns.

stem: The picture shows the path of a girl who starts at S and walks along the arrows. How many left turns (anticlockwise quarter turns) does she make along the whole path?
solution: The directions are N → E → E → E → N → N → W → W → N → N → E. Each left turn is N→W, W→S, S→E or E→N. There are 2 left turns.

stem: Early in the morning, just after sunrise, Ritu jogs with the sun on her left side. In which direction is she jogging? (The sun rises in the East.)
solution: The sun is in the East. When you face South, your left side is East. So Ritu is jogging towards the South.

stem: In the evening, just before sunset, Rohit jogs with the sun on his right side. In which direction is he jogging? (The sun sets in the West.)
solution: The sun is in the West. When you face South, your right side is West. So Rohit is jogging towards the South.

stem: A token starts at the green square S (bottom-left) and moves one square at a time, only Up or Right. It cannot enter a grey square. How many white squares (other than S) can the token NEVER reach?
solution: Mark the squares the token can reach, moving up or right and skipping grey squares. Count the white squares that never get marked.

stem: A token starts at the green square S (bottom-left) and moves one square at a time, only Up or Right. It cannot enter a grey square. How many white squares (other than S) can the token NEVER reach?
solution: Mark the squares the token can reach, moving up or right and skipping grey squares. Count the white squares that never get marked.

stem: Sam stands facing North. He walks 5 steps forward. Then he turns right and walks 3 steps, turns right again and walks 2 steps, then turns left and walks 4 steps. How many steps East of his starting point is he now?
solution: Facing North: 5 steps North. Turn right (East): 3 steps East. Turn right (South): 2 steps South. Turn left (East): 4 steps East. East in total = 3 + 4 = 7 steps.

stem: Bob stands facing East. He walks 6 steps forward. Then he turns left and walks 4 steps, turns left again and walks 2 steps, then turns right and walks 5 steps. How many steps North of his starting point is he now?
solution: Facing East: 6 steps East. Turn left (North): 4 steps North. Turn left (West): 2 steps West. Turn right (North): 5 steps North. North in total = 4 + 5 = 9 steps.

stem: Three cars A, B and C all start facing North. Car A turns right and then left. Car B turns left and then left again. Car C turns right two times. Which cars are facing in the same direction at the end?
solution: A: right then left cancel out, so A faces North. B: two lefts make a half turn, so B faces South. C: two rights (N → E → S) make a half turn, so C faces South. So B and C face the same direction.

stem: Three cars D, E and F all start facing East. Car D turns left, then right, then right again. Car E turns right two times. Car F turns left three times. Which cars are facing in the same direction at the end?
solution: D: left (North), right (East), right (South), so D faces South. E: two rights make a half turn, so E faces West. F: three lefts (East → North → West → South), so F faces South. So D and F face the same direction.

stem: Airplane A flies 30 km North and then 20 km West from an airport. Airplane B flies km North and then 20 km West from the same airport. How far apart are the two airplanes?
solution: Both airplanes end up 20 km West of the airport's North–South line, so they are directly North–South of each other. The difference in how far North they are is 45 − 30 = 15 km.

stem: Airplane P flies 25 km East and then 18 km South from an airport. Airplane Q flies 25 km East and then 40 km South from the same airport. How far apart are the two airplanes?
solution: Both airplanes are 25 km East of the airport, so they are directly North–South of each other. The difference in how far South they are is 40 − 18 = 22 km.

stem: Each shape stands for a whole number. The total of each row is given. What is the value of one star + one circle + one square?
solution: Row 1: 3 stars = 27, so a star = 9. Row 2: 9 + 2 circles = 17, so a circle = 4. Row 3: 4 + 2 squares = 10, so a square = 3. Sum = 9 + 4 + 3 = 16.

stem: Each shape stands for a whole number. The total of each row is given. What is the value of one circle?
solution: Row 1: 4 triangles = 28, so a triangle = 7. Row 2: 7 + 2 squares = 19, so a square = 6. Row 3: 6 + 3 circles = 21, so a circle = 5.

stem: The picture shows the number of trees planted by two teams. A full tree stands for trees and a half tree stands for 5 trees. How many more trees did Team A plant than Team B? Team A Team B Full tree = 10 trees, half tree = 5 trees
solution: Team A: 3 full + 1 half = 30 + 5 = 35 trees. Team B: 2 full + 1 half = 20 + 5 = 25 trees. Difference = 35 − 25 = 10.

stem: The picture shows the number of trees planted by three teams. A full tree stands for 10 trees and a half tree stands for 5 trees. How many trees did the three teams plant in all? Team X Team Y Team Z Full tree = 10 trees, half tree = 5 trees
solution: Team X: 2 full + 1 half = 25. Team Y: 1 full + 1 half = 15. Team Z: 3 full = 30. Total = 25 + 15 + 30 = 70.

stem: The table shows how many bags, boxes and caps a company packed on each day. On which day were the most items packed in all? Day Bags Boxes Caps Mon 12 8 15 Tue 10 14 9 Wed 16 7 11 Thu 9 12 18 Fri 13 10 6
