stem: The full deck has 32 cards. The statements are: "Pink is ON", "Green is ON" and "Blue is OFF". How many cards stay in the deck after all three?
solution: Each statement halves the deck: 32 → 16 → 8 → 4. The remaining cards can differ only in Yellow and Red, so 2 × 2 = 4 cards.

stem: Red is OFF, Green is ON, and Blue can be anything. How is this written as a pattern RGB = ? ? ??
solution: OFF is written O, ON is written U, and "can be anything" is written X. Red OFF = O, Green ON = U, Blue anything = X: O U X.

stem: All three lights Red, Green and Blue are ON except Green, which is OFF. Which pattern shows this?
solution: Red ON = U, Green OFF = O, Blue ON = U. So the pattern is U O U.

stem: Three statements are given about the Red, Green and Blue lights: I. The Green light is ON II. The Blue light is OFF III. Red and Green are not both ON Which card is left after all three statements are used?
solution: Statement I keeps cards with Green ON, statement II keeps those with Blue OFF: U U O and O U O. Statement III throws away U U O (Red and Green both ON). Only O U O is left.

stem: Three statements are given about the Red, Green and Blue lights: I. The Blue light is ON II. Exactly two lights are ON III. The Red light is OFF Which card is left after all three statements are used?
solution: Statement I keeps cards with Blue ON: U U U, U O U, O U U, O O U. Statement II keeps those with exactly two ON: U O U and O U U. Statement III throws away U O U (Red ON). Only O U U is left.

stem: Form the largest four-digit odd number by taking exactly one digit from each row and each column. The digit from the 1st row is the thousands digit, the 2nd row the hundreds, the 3rd row the tens and the 4th row the ones. What is the sum of the digits of that number?
solution: The ones digit (4th row) must be odd. Try the biggest digits first for the thousands and hundreds places while keeping every column different. The best choice gives 9835, and its digit sum is 9 + 8 + 3 + 5 = 25.

stem: Form the largest four-digit odd number by taking exactly one digit from each row and each column. The digit from the 1st row is the thousands digit, the 2nd row the hundreds, the 3rd row the tens and the 4th row the ones. What is the sum of the digits of that number?
solution: The ones digit (4th row) must be odd. Try the biggest digits first for the thousands and hundreds places while keeping every column different. The best choice gives 8985, and its digit sum is 8 + 9 + 8 + 5 = 30.

stem: S, T and N are three different single digits, with S and the first digit of every number not zero, and T > S. If ST + TS = NSN (ST and TS are two-digit numbers, NSN is a three-digit number), what is the value of N + T?
solution: ST + TS = 11 × (S + T), so NSN must be a multiple of 11 that is below 200, which gives 121 (S + T = 11). So N = 1, S = 2, T = 9: 29 + 92 = 121. N + T = 10.

stem: S, T and N are three different single digits, with S not zero and T > S. If ST × ST = TNT (ST is a two-digit number, TNT is a three-digit number), what is the value of N + T?
solution: The last digit of ST × ST equals T, so T is 0, 1, 5 or 6. Testing the squares gives 26 × 26 = 676. So S = 2, T = 6, N = 7 and N + T = 13.

stem: Fill each box with a different digit from 1 to 9 so that the sum of every row and every column is 15, and every sign (< or >, read left-to-right or top-to-bottom) between two boxes is true. What are the values of A and B?
solution: Use the sums of 15 and the signs to fix the digits one by one. The only grid that works is (rows) 8 4 3 / 1 9 5 / 6 2 7. So A = 3 and B = 9.

stem: Fill each box with a different digit from 1 to 9 so that the sum of every row and every column is 15, and every sign (< or >, read left-to-right or top-to-bottom) between two boxes is true. What are the values of A and B?
solution: Use the sums of 15 and the signs to fix the digits one by one. The only grid that works is (rows) 5 9 1 / 3 4 8 / 7 2 6. So A = 2 and B = 3.

stem: How many cells contain a digit that is equal to the sum of all the other digits in its own row and its own column combined?
solution: For each cell add the other numbers in its row and column and compare. These cells match: row 1, column 2: 7 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 1; row 3, column 1: 5 = 1 + 2 + 1 + 1. That is 2 cells.

stem: How many cells contain a digit that is equal to the sum of all the other digits in its own row and its own column combined?
solution: For each cell add the other numbers in its row and column and compare. These cells match: row 1, column 3: 7 = 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1; row 3, column 1: 7 = 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1; row 4, column 4: 8 = 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2. That is 3 cells.

stem: Using the digits 2, 5, 7, 9 (a digit may be used more than once), form the highest and the smallest three-digit numbers that each contain exactly two different digits. What is the sum of the two numbers?
solution: Highest: use the biggest digit twice and the next biggest once, with the biggest digits first: 997. Smallest: use the smallest digit twice and the next smallest once, with the smallest digit first: 225. Sum = 997 + 225 = 1222.

stem: Using the digits 1, 3, 6, 8 (a digit may be used more than once), form the highest and the smallest three-digit numbers that each contain exactly two different digits. What is the sum of the two numbers?
solution: Highest: use the biggest digit twice and the next biggest once, with the biggest digits first: 886. Smallest: use the smallest digit twice and the next smallest once, with the smallest digit first: 113. Sum = 886 + 113 = 999.

stem: A two-digit number is formed with two different non-zero digits. The digits are reversed to make another two-digit number. The difference of the two numbers is always a multiple of which of these?
solution: The difference of ab and ba is 9 × (a − b), so it is always a multiple of 9. Check: 12 and 21 give 9, 35 and 53 give 18; both are multiples of 9.

stem: A two-digit number is formed with two different non-zero digits. The digits are reversed to make another two-digit number. The sum of the two numbers is always a multiple of which of these?
solution: The sum of ab and ba is 11 × (a + b), so it is always a multiple of 11. Check: 12 and 21 give 33, 35 and 53 give 88; both are multiples of 11.

stem: A 4-digit number has the same number of even and odd digits (2 of each). Which of these could be the sum of its digits?
solution: Two odd digits add to an even number, and the even digits add to an even number, so the digit sum must be even. Only 30 is even and also reachable (the largest possible sum is 34).

stem: A 6-digit number has the same number of even and odd digits (3 of each). Which of these could be the sum of its digits?
solution: Three odd digits add to an odd number, and the even digits add to an even number, so the digit sum must be odd. Only 41 is odd and also reachable (the largest possible sum is 51).

stem: Fill the grid with different single-digit natural numbers so that the sum of each row is the same and is an even number, and the larger number of each column is in the red box. What is the sum of the numbers in the three white boxes?
solution: The two rows have equal even sums, and each red box holds the larger number of its column. Testing the given numbers against these rules leaves only one fit for the white boxes, and they add up to 8.

stem: Fill the grid with different single-digit natural numbers so that the sum of each row is the same and is an even number, and the larger number of each column is in the red box. What is the sum of the numbers in the three white boxes?
solution: The two rows have equal even sums, and each red box holds the larger number of its column. Testing the given numbers against these rules leaves only one fit for the white boxes, and they add up to 12.

stem: A computer draws rectangles whose length and breadth follow a pattern. If the pattern continues, what will be the area of the next rectangle?
solution: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, 29. The next rectangle is 18 × 29, with area 522 sq. units.

stem: A computer draws rectangles whose length and breadth follow a pattern. If the pattern continues, what will be the area of the next rectangle?
solution: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 2, 5, 7, 12, 19, 31, 50. The next rectangle is 31 × 50, with area 1550 sq. units.

stem: Fill the 3 × 3 grid with the numbers 1 to 9, each used once, so that every pair of neighbouring numbers in a row differs by 3. Some numbers are already placed. What number goes in the cell marked ?
solution: A row with neighbours differing by 3 must be 1, 4, 7 or 2, 5, 8 or 3, 6, 9 (in either order). Using the given numbers to decide which row is which, the grid is (rows) 9 6 3 / 1 4 7 / 8 5 2. So ? = 2.

stem: Fill the 3 × 3 grid with the numbers 1 to 9, each used once, so that every pair of neighbouring numbers in a row differs by 3. Some numbers are already placed. What number goes in the cell marked ?
solution: A row with neighbours differing by 3 must be 1, 4, 7 or 2, 5, 8 or 3, 6, 9 (in either order). Using the given numbers to decide which row is which, the grid is (rows) 1 4 7 / 3 6 9 / 2 5 8. So ? = 7.

stem: 6 bulbs are in a row, each with a switch beneath it. When a switch is pressed it lights up only the two neighbouring bulbs (left and right) and not the bulb right above the switch. What is the minimum number of switches you must press to light up all 6 bulbs?
solution: The end bulbs can only be lit by switches 2 and 5, so both must be pressed. Check the rest and add switches only for bulbs still dark; the smallest working set has 4 presses.

stem: 9 bulbs are in a row, each with a switch beneath it. When a switch is pressed it lights up only the two neighbouring bulbs (left and right) and not the bulb right above the switch. What is the minimum number of switches you must press to light up all 9 bulbs?
solution: The end bulbs can only be lit by switches 2 and 8, so both must be pressed. Check the rest and add switches only for bulbs still dark; the smallest working set has 5 presses.

stem: A square and an equilateral triangle have the same perimeter of 24 cm. Which statement is true about their areas?
options: The triangle has the greater area
The square has the greater area
solution: The square has side 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm, so its area is 36 sq. cm. The triangle has side 24 ÷ 3 = 8 cm, and its area is (√3 ÷ 4) × 8 × 8 ≈ 27.7 sq. cm. So the square has the greater area.

stem: A regular hexagon and an equilateral triangle have sides of the same length. The area of the hexagon is how many times the area of the triangle?
solution: Join the centre of the hexagon to its corners. It splits into 6 equilateral triangles, each with the same side as the given triangle. So the hexagon is 6 times as large.

stem: 25 identical small equilateral triangles are joined edge to edge, with no gaps or overlaps, to make one big equilateral triangle. How many small triangles lie along each side of the big triangle?
solution: A big triangle with n small triangles along each side has n × n small triangles in all. 5 × 5 = 25, so n = 5.

stem: An equilateral triangle of side 12 cm is cut into small equilateral triangles of side 3 cm, with no waste. How many small triangles are there?
solution: Each side holds 12 ÷ 3 = 4 small triangles, and the whole figure has 4 × 4 = 16 small triangles.

stem: How many different triangles can be made with a perimeter of 13 cm, if every side is whole number of cm?
solution: List the sides in order a ≤ b ≤ c with a + b + c = 13, and keep those where a + b > c (two sides together must be longer than the third). They are 1-6-6, 2-5-6, 3-4-6, 3-5-5, 4-4-5. That is 5 triangles.

stem: How many different scalene (all three sides different) triangles can be made with a perimeter of 15 cm, if every side is a whole number of cm?
solution: List the sides in order a ≤ b ≤ c with a + b + c = 15, and keep those where a + b > c (two sides together must be longer than the third). They are 2-6-7, 3-5-7, 4-5-6. That is 3 triangles.

stem: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 31 cm and all its sides are whole numbers of cm. The two equal sides are multiples of 4. How many different lengths can the third side have?
solution: Try equal sides of 4, 8, 12, … and keep those where the third side is positive and the two equal sides together are longer than it. That gives: equal sides 8 cm → third side 15 cm, equal sides 12 cm → third side 7 cm. So 2 different lengths.

stem: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 40 cm and all its sides are whole numbers of cm. The two equal sides are multiples of 3. How many different lengths can the third side have?
solution: Try equal sides of 3, 6, 9, … and keep those where the third side is positive and the two equal sides together are longer than it. That gives: equal sides 12 cm → third side 16 cm, equal sides 15 cm → third side 10 cm, equal sides 18 cm → third side 4 cm. So 3 different lengths.

stem: Is triangle ABC an equilateral triangle? Information 1: Triangle ABC is isosceles. Information 2: One of the angles of triangle ABC is 60°. Which of the given information is/are sufficient to answer the question?
options: Only 2 Question cannot be answered even if both
solution: Alone, neither works: an isosceles triangle need not be equilateral, and a triangle with one 60° angle can be scalene. Together: an isosceles triangle has two equal angles. If the 60° angle is one of them, the other equal angle is also 60° and the third is 60°. If the 60° angle is the odd one, the two equal angles are (180 − 60) ÷ 2 = 60° each. In both cases all three angles are 60°, so it is equilateral.

stem: Are triangles X and Y similar? Information 1: All three pairs of corresponding sides of X and Y are in the ratio 2 : 3. Information 2: One pair of corresponding angles is equal, and one pair of corresponding sides is in the ratio 2 : 3. Which of the given information is/are sufficient to answer the question?
options: Only 2 Question cannot be answered even if both
solution: Information 1 gives all three sides in the same ratio, which is enough for similar triangles (same shape). Information 2 gives only one angle and one side ratio, which is not enough, because the other sides could be anything. So only Information 1 is sufficient.

stem: The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. What is the measure of the largest angle?
solution: The ratio parts add to 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, and the angles add to 180°, so one part is 30°. The angles are 30°, 60° and 90°. The largest is 90°.

stem: An isosceles triangle has one angle of 100°. What is the measure of each of the other two angles?
solution: The 100° angle cannot be a base angle, because then two angles would add to 200°. So the two equal angles share the remaining 180° − 100° = 80°, which is 40° each.

stem: How many right-angled triangles of all sizes can be found in this figure?
solution: Count triangles by size, then keep those with a right angle. The two diagonals cut the square into 4 small triangles, and each half of the square (cut by one diagonal) is also a triangle: 4 + 4 = 8, all with a right angle.

stem: How many right-angled triangles of all sizes can be found in this figure?
solution: Count triangles by size, then keep those with a right angle. Counting every triangle formed by three of the lines gives 16 triangles in all, and 16 of them have a 90° angle.

stem: A triangle has 3 points marked on its base, and each point is joined to the top corner by a straight line, as shown. How many triangles of all sizes are in the figure?
solution: Every triangle has the top corner and two of the 5 points on the base (the 3 marked points and the two ends). That gives 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 triangles.

stem: A triangle has 5 points marked on its base, and each point is joined to the top corner by a straight line, as shown. How many triangles of all sizes are in the figure?
solution: Every triangle has the top corner and two of the 7 points on the base (the 5 marked points and the two ends). That gives 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 triangles.

stem: Triangle ABC has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. Triangle PQR is similar to ABC, and the shortest side of PQR is 9 cm. What is the perimeter of PQR?
solution: Similar triangles have all sides in the same ratio. 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5. So PQR has sides 9, 12, 15 cm, and its perimeter is 36 cm.

stem: Triangle ABC has sides 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm. Triangle PQR is similar to ABC, and the middle side of PQR is 18 cm. What is the perimeter of PQR?
solution: Similar triangles have all sides in the same ratio. 18 ÷ 12 = 1.5. So PQR has sides 7.5, 18, 19.5 cm, and its perimeter is 45 cm.

stem: An equilateral triangle is cut along one of its altitudes (a line from a corner perpendicular to the opposite side). One of the two pieces is then cut along the altitude drawn from its right-angle corner to the longest side. How many right-angled triangles are there in total now?
solution: The first cut gives 2 right-angled triangles. Cutting one of them along the altitude to its longest side gives 2 more right-angled triangles in its place. So the total is 1 + 2 = 3.

stem: An equilateral triangle is cut along one altitude into 2 right-angled triangles. Each piece is then cut along the altitude drawn from its right-angle corner to its longest side. How many right-angled triangles are there in total now?
solution: Each of the 2 right-angled pieces is replaced by 2 smaller right-angled triangles when it is cut along its altitude to the longest side. So 2 × 2 = 4 triangles.

stem: A 3 × 3 grid is shown. You may place a circle in any cell, but no three circles may be in a straight line — in a row, a column or a diagonal — next to each other. What is the maximum number of circles you can place?
solution: Checking arrangements, a row of 3 neighbouring circles is never allowed, so each row can hold at most 2 of every 3 cells in a line. The best arrangement that also avoids columns and diagonals has 6 circles, and adding one more always makes three in a line.

stem: A 3 × 4 grid is shown. You may place a circle in any cell, but no three circles may be in a straight line — in a row, a column or a diagonal — next to each other. What is the maximum number of circles you can place?
solution: Checking arrangements, a row of 3 neighbouring circles is never allowed, so each row can hold at most 2 of every 3 cells in a line. The best arrangement that also avoids columns and diagonals has 7 circles, and adding one more always makes three in a line.

stem: Maya received sweets for a festival and shared them with the family. • Maya keeps 2/5 of the sweets. • Maya gives 1/3 of what is left to Neha. • The remaining 18 sweets go to Omar. How many sweets did Maya receive in all?
solution: After keeping 2/5, 3/5 of the sweets are left. Neha gets 1/3 of that, which is 1/5 of all. What is left is 3/5 − 1/5 = 2/5 of all, and this is 18. So all = 18 ÷ 2/5 = 45.

stem: Kabir received sweets for a festival and shared them with the family. • Kabir keeps 1/4 of the sweets. • Kabir gives 2/5 of what is left to Tara. • The remaining 27 sweets go to Dev. How many sweets did Kabir receive in all?
solution: After keeping 1/4, 3/4 of the sweets are left. Tara gets 2/5 of that, which is 3/10 of all. What is left is 3/4 − 3/10 = 9/20 of all, and this is 27. So all = 27 ÷ 9/20 = 60.

stem: A bus starts from Delhi with some passengers. • At Agra, 1/3 of the passengers get off and 24 new passengers get on. • At Jaipur, 1/2 of the passengers get off and nobody gets on. The bus leaves Jaipur with 52 passengers. How many passengers boarded the bus Delhi?
solution: Work backwards. After Jaipur there are 52; before Jaipur it had 52 ÷ (1 − 1/2) = 104. Before the 24 got on at Agra: 104 − 24 = 80. That is (1 − 1/3) of the start, so the start = 80 ÷ 2/3 = 120.

stem: A bus starts from Delhi with some passengers. • At Agra, 1/5 of the passengers get off and 30 new passengers get on. • At Jaipur, 1/3 of the passengers get off and nobody gets on. The bus leaves Jaipur with 60 passengers. How many passengers boarded the bus Delhi?
solution: Work backwards. After Jaipur there are 60; before Jaipur it had 60 ÷ (1 − 1/3) = 90. Before the 30 got on at Agra: 90 − 30 = 60. That is (1 − 1/5) of the start, so the start = 60 ÷ 4/5 = 75.

stem: Which of the following statements is/are sufficient to answer the question? Question: What fraction of the water in a tank is used on Monday and Tuesday together? Statement 1: The tank holds 600 litres. Statement 2: On Monday, one-fourth of the water is used. Statement 3: On Tuesday, one-third of the water that was left after Monday is used.
solution: The tank size (Statement 1) does not matter because we want a fraction. Monday uses 1/4. Tuesday uses 1/3 of the remaining 3/4, which is 1/4 of the whole. Together 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. So both Statement 2 and Statement 3 are needed.

stem: Which of the following statements is/are sufficient to answer the question? Question: What fraction of the cake did Riya eat? Statement 1: Riya ate 2 pieces more than Dev. Statement 2: Dev ate one-sixth of the whole cake. Statement 3: The cake was cut into equal pieces.
solution: Dev ate 1/6 of the cake, and Riya ate 2 more pieces than Dev. But we are never told how many pieces the cake has, so we cannot turn "2 pieces" into a fraction. Even with all three statements the question cannot be answered.

stem: A square farm is divided into equal small squares and used as shown. What fraction of the whole farm is covered by wheat?
solution: 4 of the 16 small squares are wheat, which is 4/16 = 1/4.

stem: A square farm is divided into equal small squares and used as shown. What fraction of the whole farm is in use (rice, wheat or water, but not unused)?
solution: The unused squares number 4, so 16 − 4 = 12 squares are in use. That is 12/16 = 3/4.

stem: A wire is bent into a rectangle of length L and breadth B. Later the length is increased by 1/4 of its original value and the breadth is decreased by 1/4 of its original value. After this change the perimeter is the same, and the area has decreased by 36 sq. cm. What was the original length?
solution: The perimeter stays the same only if the length gained equals the breadth lost: L/4 = B/4, so L = B (a square). The new area is (1 + 1/4)(1 − 1/4) L² = 15/16 L², so the area falls by L²/16 = 36. Then L² = 576 and L = 24 cm.

stem: A wire is bent into a rectangle of length L and breadth B. Later the length is increased by 1/10 of its original value and the breadth is decreased by 1/10 of its original value. After this change the perimeter is the same, and the area has decreased by 49 sq. cm. What was the original length?
solution: The perimeter stays the same only if the length gained equals the breadth lost: L/10 = B/10, so L = B (a square). The new area is (1 + 1/10)(1 − 1/10) L² = 99/100 L², so the area falls by L²/100 = 49. Then L² = 4900 and L = 70 cm.

stem: A sequence of fractions is given:
solution: Each term is the one before multiplied by 2/3 (top × 2, bottom × 3). The k-th term equals 45/4 × (2/3)^(k−1). Its value is 11.25, then 7.50, 5.00, 3.33, 2.22, 1.48, 0.99. The first value below 1 is the 7th term.

stem: A sequence of fractions is given:
solution: Each term is the one before multiplied by 3/4 (top × 3, bottom × 4). The k-th term equals 100/9 × (3/4)^(k−1). Its value is 11.11, then 8.33, 6.25, 4.69, 3.52, 2.64, 1.98, 1.48, 1.11, 0.83. The first value below 1 is the 10th term.

stem: A box has 150 chalks. Each day a teacher uses one chalk. When a chalk has worn down to 1/6 of its original size, she sets it aside. Whenever she has enough of these small pieces to make one full chalk, she joins them and uses it. For how many days will the 150 chalks last?
solution: 150 chalk(s) last 150 day(s); the stubs make 25 new chalk(s); 25 chalk(s) last 25 day(s); the stubs make 4 new chalk(s); 4 chalk(s) last 4 day(s). The total is 179 days.

stem: A box has 64 chalks. Each day a teacher uses one chalk. When a chalk has worn down to 1/4 of its original size, she sets it aside. Whenever she has enough of these small pieces to make one full chalk, she joins them and uses it. For how many days will the 64 chalks last?
solution: 64 chalk(s) last 64 day(s); the stubs make 16 new chalk(s); 16 chalk(s) last 16 day(s); the stubs make 4 new chalk(s); 4 chalk(s) last 4 day(s); the stubs make 1 new chalk(s); 1 chalk(s) last 1 day(s). The total is 85 days.

stem: A grid has apples and flowers in its cells. A 3 × 3 square frame covers exactly 9 cells and can be placed (without turning) anywhere inside the grid. In how many different positions will at least one-third of the 9 covered cells be flowers?
solution: One-third of 9 is 3, so a position needs 3 or more flowers. The 6 positions (top-left cell of the frame: flowers) give (1,1): 1, (1,2): 1, (1,3): 2, (2,1): 4, (2,2): 3, (2,3): 3. 3 of them have 3 or more flowers.

stem: A grid has apples and flowers in its cells. A 3 × 3 square frame covers exactly 9 cells and can be placed (without turning) anywhere inside the grid. In how many different positions will at least one-third of the 9 covered cells be flowers?
solution: One-third of 9 is 3, so a position needs 3 or more flowers. The 9 positions (top-left cell of the frame: flowers) give (1,1): 1, (1,2): 1, (1,3): 2, (2,1): 1, (2,2): 1, (2,3): 3, (3,1): 3, (3,2): 3, (3,3): 3. 4 of them have 3 or more flowers.

stem: Each circle is divided into equal parts, and some parts are shaded. A fraction is written under each circle. How many of these fractions correctly show the shaded part of their circle?
solution: 3 of 8 parts shaded = 3/8, written 3/8: correct; 2 of 6 parts shaded = 2/6, written 1/3: correct; 4 of 5 parts shaded = 4/5, written 4/9: wrong; 1 of 4 parts shaded = 1/4, written 2/8: correct; 6 of 10 parts shaded = 6/10, written 3/5: correct. So 4 are correct.

stem: Each circle is divided into equal parts, and some parts are shaded. A fraction is written under each circle. How many of these fractions correctly show the shaded part of their circle?
solution: 5 of 6 parts shaded = 5/6, written 5/6: correct; 2 of 8 parts shaded = 2/8, written 1/4: correct; 2 of 3 parts shaded = 2/3, written 2/5: wrong; 3 of 9 parts shaded = 3/9, written 1/3: correct. So 3 are correct.

stem: A water tank is 3/5 full. After 30 litres more are poured in, it is 4/5 full. How many litres can the tank hold when full?
solution: The extra 30 litres fill 4/5 − 3/5 = 1/5 of the tank. So the full tank holds 30 × 5 = 150 litres.

stem: Rahul reads 2/7 of a book on the first day and 1/3 of the remaining pages on the second day. He still has 80 pages left. How many pages does the book have?
solution: After day 1, 5/7 of the book is left. On day 2 he reads 1/3 of that, so 2/3 of 5/7 = 10/21 of the book is still left. 10/21 of the book = 80 pages, so the whole book = 80 × 21 ÷ 10 = 168 pages.

stem: 10 squares are arranged in a row, as shown. What is the minimum number of swaps needed so that black and white squares alternate? (Swapping one black square with one white square counts as 1 swap.)
solution: Compare the row with BWBW… and WBWB…. Count the squares in the wrong colour. Each swap fixes two wrong squares (one black and one white). The better pattern has 4 wrong squares, so it needs 2 swaps.

stem: Sam writes a list of natural numbers. The list has 4 perfect cubes and 5 perfect squares, and no number in the list has more than two digits. What is the minimum number of distinct numbers he must have written?
solution: A number that is both a square and a cube is a perfect 6th power. Up to two digits these are 1, 64. Each of them can count as a cube and a square at once, saving one number each. So 4 + 5 − 2 = 7.

stem: Sam writes a list of natural numbers. The list has 5 perfect cubes and 6 perfect squares, and no number in the list has more than three digits. What is the minimum number of distinct numbers he must have written?
solution: A number that is both a square and a cube is a perfect 6th power. Up to three digits these are 1, 64, 729. Each of them can count as a cube and a square at once, saving one number each. So 5 + 6 − 3 = 8.

stem: 180 × k is a perfect cube, where k is a natural number. What is the smallest possible value of k?
solution: Split 180 into primes: 2^2 × 3^2 × 5. In a perfect cube every prime appears a multiple of 3 times. Add the missing primes: k = 150. Check: 180 × 150 = 27000 = 30³.

stem: What is the smallest natural number by which 2160 must be divided so that the quotient is a perfect cube?
solution: 2160 = 2^4 × 3^3 × 5. Remove the extra primes that do not fill a group of 3: divide by 10. The quotient is 216 = 6³.

stem: XYZ is a 3-digit number that is the square of a multiple of 4. What is the highest possible remainder when XYZ is divided by 100?
solution: The 3-digit squares of multiples of 4 are 144, 256, 400, 576, 784. Their remainders on division by 100 are 44, 56, 0, 76, 84. The highest is 84.

stem: How many 4-digit perfect cubes have an odd last digit?
solution: The 4-digit cubes are the cubes of 10 to 21: 1000, 1331, 1728, 2197, 2744, 3375, 4096, 4913, 5832, 6859, 8000, 9261. A cube has an odd last digit only when the number cubed is odd (11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 21). That is 6 cubes.

stem: A teacher writes this pattern on the board:
solution: The pattern is n³ − (n − 1)³ = 3 × n × (n − 1) + 1. For n = 22: 3 × 22 × 21 + 1. The digits used are 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, so the digit 2 appears 3 times, more than any other.

stem: A teacher writes this pattern on the board:
solution: The pattern is n³ − (n − 1)³ = 3 × n × (n − 1) + 1. For n = 31: 3 × 31 × 30 + 1. The digits used are 3, 3, 1, 3, 0, 1, so the digit 3 appears 3 times, more than any other.

stem: AB is a two-digit number whose square is a 4-digit number ending in the digit C, such that B < A < C. How many different values can C take?
solution: List the two-digit numbers AB whose square has 4 digits, and compare B < A < C where C is the last digit of the {nm}: 32² = 1024 (C = 4); 43² = 1849 (C = 9); 53² = 2809 (C = 9); 54² = 2916 (C = 6); 63² = 3969 (C = 9); 73² = 5329 (C = 9); 83² = 6889 (C = 9); 87² = 7569 (C = 9). The values of C are 4, 6, 9: 3 different values.

stem: AB is a two-digit number whose cube is a 4-digit number ending in the digit C, such that A < C < B. How many different values can C take?
solution: List the two-digit numbers AB whose cube has 4 digits, and compare A < C < B where C is the last digit of the {nm}: 17³ = 4913 (C = 3); 18³ = 5832 (C = 2). The values of C are 2, 3: 2 different values.

stem: A secret operation ⊕ works the same way each time:
solution: Test each example: 2 ⊕ 3 = 2² + 3³ = 31, 3 ⊕ 2 = 3² + 2³ = 17, 1 ⊕ 4 = 1² + 4³ = 65. So a ⊕ b = a² + b³. Then 4 ⊕ 3 = 4² + 3³ = 43.

stem: A secret operation ⊗ works the same way each time:
solution: Test each example: 4 ⊗ 3 = 4³ − 3² = 55, 3 ⊗ 2 = 3³ − 2² = 23, 5 ⊗ 4 = 5³ − 4² = 109. So a ⊗ b = a³ − b². Then 6 ⊗ 2 = 6³ − 2² = 212.

stem: In a number machine, an input passes through 3 tunnels, and each tunnel changes it in a different way: Tunnel 1: the number is squared Tunnel 2: the number is decreased by 5 Tunnel 3: the number is squared The inputs 3, 4 and 5 are put in. What is the sum of the outputs?

In a number machine, an input passes through 4 tunnels, and each tunnel changes it in a different way: Tunnel 1: the number is squared Tunnel 2: the number is increased by 15 Tunnel 3: the number is replaced by its square root Tunnel 4: the number is cubed The inputs 1 and 7 are put in. What is the sum of the outputs?
Every column in the table follows the same rule. What number should replace ?
solution: In each column the top number is n, the middle is n² + 1, and the bottom is n³ + n. For n = 5: 5³ + 5 = 130.

stem: Every column in the table follows the same rule. What number should replace ?
solution: In each column the middle number is the cube of the top number, and the bottom is that cube minus the square of the top. For n = 6: 6³ − 6² = 180.

stem: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n. What is the sum of all the odd numbers from 21 to 41?
solution: Odd numbers up to 41 are the first 21 odd numbers, which sum to 21² = 441. The odd numbers below 21 are the first 10, which sum to 10² = 100. So 441 − 100 = 341.

stem: How many perfect squares lie between 500 and 5000?
solution: 22² = 484 is below 500 and 23² = 529 is above it. 70² = 4900 is below 5000 and 71² = 5041 is above it. So the squares of 23, 24, …, 70 count: 70 − 23 + 1 = 48.

stem: A solid cube of side 6 cm is painted on all its faces and then cut into 216 small cubes side 1 cm. How many small cubes have exactly two faces painted?
solution: Cubes with two painted faces lie along the 12 edges, excluding the 2 corner cubes at the ends of each edge. Each edge has 6 − 2 = 4 such cubes, so 12 × 4 = 48.

stem: A solid cube of side 7 cm is painted on all its faces and then cut into 343 small cubes of side 1 cm. How many small cubes have no face painted?
solution: The cubes with no painted face form a smaller cube inside, with 7 − 2 = 5 cubes along each edge. So 5³ = 125.

stem: Boxes are stacked in four columns A, B, C and D, with labels 1, 2 or 3: • Some labels are already shown • No two boxes that are one above the other have the same label • No two neighbouring columns have the same number on the topmost box • In every column, the sum of the top and bottom labels is the same Which number occurs the greatest number of times in the shaded boxes?
solution: Use the rules to fill the boxes one at a time. The only complete arrangement is (top row first) 3 2 3 2 / 1 1 1 1 / 2 3 2 3. The shaded boxes hold 3, 3, 3, so the number 3 occurs most often.

stem: A team is to be formed from 7 students: A, B, C, D, E, F, G. • A and B cannot both be in the team, but one of them must be • C and D are either both in or both out • E and F are either both in or both out If the team has 5 students, in how many different ways can it be formed?
solution: Pick exactly one of A and B. The other 4 members come from C, D, E, F, G, where C and D go together and E and F go together. The valid teams are: ACDEF; BCDEF. That is 2 ways.

stem: A team is to be formed from 6 students: P, Q, R, S, T, U. • P and Q cannot be together • R and S are either both in or both out • at least one of T and U must be in the team If the team has 3 students, in how many different ways can it be formed?
solution: Check each team of 3 against the three rules. The valid teams are: PTU; QTU; RST; RSU. That is 4 ways.

stem: X, Y and Z are single-digit whole numbers. XY is the two-digit number formed by the digits X and Y, and Z is at least 2. If 6000 < (XY)^Z < 7000, what is the minimum possible value of XY?
solution: Try each exponent Z. The two-digit numbers that work are: 19^3 = 6859, 78^2 = 6084, 79^2 = 6241, 80^2 = 6400, 81^2 = 6561, 82^2 = 6724, 83^2 = 6889. The smallest XY is 19.

stem: X, Y and Z are single-digit whole numbers. XY is the two-digit number formed by the digits X and Y, and Z is at least 2. If 2000 < (XY)^Z < 3000, what is the maximum possible value of XY?

Raj picks one number from each row of the table. The numbers are written as powers (base and exponent). The rule is that no digit is repeated among all the bases and exponents of the three numbers he picks. What is the sum of the values of the three numbers?
solution: Row R1 has only powers of 3, so the base 3 is used. Try each pick from R2 and R3 and reject any that repeats a digit. The only choice that works is 3⁵ = 243, 8⁴ = 4096, 7² = 49. The sum is 4388.

stem: Raj picks one number from each row of the table. The numbers are written as powers (base and exponent). The rule is that no digit is repeated among all the bases and exponents of the three numbers he picks. What is the sum of the values of the three numbers?
solution: Row R1 has only powers of 3, so the base 3 is used. Try each pick from R2 and R3 and reject any that repeats a digit. The only choice that works is 3⁴ = 81, 6² = 36, 7⁵ = 16807. The sum is 16924.

stem: A bag can carry at most 30 units. Four kinds of books can be put in it: Maths: load 4, points 24 Physics: load 3, points 15 Fiction: load 2, points 9 Management: load 5, points 20 • For every Maths book there must be 2 Physics books • For every Management book there must be 2 Fiction books He must carry at least one book of every kind. What is the maximum number of points he can earn without going over the limit?
solution: Because of the rules, books come in sets. 2 Maths, 4 Physics, 2 Fiction, 1 Management have a load of 29 (within 30) and earn 146 points. Trying the other allowed combinations gives fewer points.

stem: A bag can carry at most 26 units. Four kinds of books can be put in it: Art: load 3, points 14 Music: load 2, points 7 Sport: load 4, points 22 Drama: load 2, points 11 • For every Art book there must be 2 Music books • For every Sport book there must be 2 Drama books He must carry at least one book of every kind. What is the maximum number of points he can earn without going over the limit?
solution: Because of the rules, books come in sets. 1 Art, 2 Music, 2 Sport, 4 Drama have a load of 23 (within 26) and earn 116 points. Trying the other allowed combinations gives fewer points.

stem: A shop sells 4 shirts, 3 trousers and 5 caps. One shirt, one trouser and one cap are chosen for an outfit. The red cap cannot be worn with the blue shirt. How many different outfits are possible?
solution: Without any restriction there are 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 outfits. Outfits with the blue shirt and the red cap: 1 × 3 × 1 = 3 (the trouser can be any of 3). So 60 − 3 = 57.

stem: A 3-digit code is made from the digits 1 to 6, with no digit repeated, and the first digit must be even. How many different codes are possible?
solution: The first digit can be 2, 4 or 6 (3 ways). The second digit can be any of the 5 remaining digits, and the third any of the 4 left. So 3 × 5 × 4 = 60.

stem: Sam has exactly ₹5000. The number of ₹1 coins is a power of 10, the number of ₹2 coins is a power of 5, the number of ₹5 coins is a power of 2, and the rest of the money is in ₹10 coins. The money in each of the ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins is at least ₹500. What is the maximum possible number of ₹10 coins?
solution: The money in ₹1 coins is 10^a, in ₹2 coins 2 × 5^b and in ₹5 coins 5 × 2^c (each at least 500). Checking every possibility and keeping those where the remaining money is a multiple of 10, the maximum count of ₹10 coins is 211, for example with 1000 one-rupee coins, 625 two-rupee coins and 128 five-rupee coins.

stem: Sam has exactly ₹3000. The number of ₹1 coins is a power of 10, the number of ₹2 coins is a power of 5, the number of ₹5 coins is a power of 2, and the rest of the money is in ₹10 coins. The money in each of the ₹1, ₹2 and ₹5 coins is at least ₹400. What is the minimum possible number of ₹10 coins?
solution: The money in ₹1 coins is 10^a, in ₹2 coins 2 × 5^b and in ₹5 coins 5 × 2^c (each at least 400). Checking every possibility and keeping those where the remaining money is a multiple of 10, the smallest count of ₹10 coins is 11.

stem: A game: Sam writes A^B , where A and B are different single-digit natural numbers with A + B = 9. He must then change his number using exactly one rule: • If the base is smaller than the exponent, replace the base n by 1/n • If the base is greater than the exponent, replace the exponent n by 1/n Sam wants his final number to be as large as possible. Which values of A and B should he choose?
solution: When A < B the new number is (1/A)^B, which is at most 1. When A > B the new number is A^(1/B). A = 8, B = 1: 8.00; A = 7, B = 2: 2.65; A = 6, B = 3: 1.82; A = 5, B = 4: 1.50. The largest final number is 8.00, with A = 8 and B = 1.

stem: A game: Sam writes A^B , where A and B are different single-digit natural numbers with A + B = 12. He must then change his number using exactly one rule: • If the base is smaller than the exponent, replace the base n by 1/n • If the base is greater than the exponent, replace the exponent n by 1/n Sam wants his final number to be as large as possible. Which values of A and B should he choose?
solution: When A < B the new number is (1/A)^B, which is at most 1. When A > B the new number is A^(1/B). A = 9, B = 3: 2.08; A = 8, B = 4: 1.68; A = 7, B = 5: 1.48; A = 3, B = 9: 0.00. The largest final number is 2.08, with A = 9 and B = 3.

stem: What is the last digit of 13^57 + 17^43 ?
solution: Only the last digits matter. Powers of 3 end in 3, 9, 7, 1 and repeat every 4; 57 = 4 × 14 + 1, so 13^57 ends in 3. Powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1; 43 = 4 × 10 + 3, so 17^43 ends in 3. The sum ends in 3 + 3 = 6.

stem: How many zeros are at the end of the number 8^15 × 25^9 ?
solution: 8^15 = 2^45 and 25^9 = 5^18. Each pair of one 2 and one 5 gives a 10, a zero at the end. There are only 18 fives, so only 18 pairs: 18 zeros.

stem: Place all of A, H, M, 4, 2, 3 in the empty squares of the 2 × 3 grid, each once, so that: • Every vowel has an even number in at least one neighbouring square • The letter H is not next to A or 3 • Two consecutive numbers are never in neighbouring squares Squares are neighbours only if they share a side. What goes in the square marked ?
solution: Test the placements against each rule. The arrangement is (top row / bottom row) A 4 H / 3 M 2. So ? = M.

label: P2
stem: Place all of A, H, E, 5, 4, 3 in the empty squares of the 2 × 3 grid, each once, so that: • Every vowel has an even number in at least one neighbouring square • The letter H is not next to A or 4 • Two consecutive numbers are never in neighbouring squares Squares are neighbours only if they share a side. What goes in the square marked ?
solution: Test the placements against each rule. The arrangement is (top row / bottom row) 5 A 4 / H 3 E. So ? = 4.

label: A1
stem: How many decimal pipes are needed to measure a person who is 84 inches tall, using the fewest pipes?
solution: Use as many 100-inch pipes, 10-inch pipes and 1-inch pipes as the digits say: 8 × 10 + 4 × 1. The number of pipes is 8 + 4 = 12.

label: A2
stem: How many decimal pipes are needed to measure a person who is 137 inches tall, using the fewest pipes?
solution: Use as many 100-inch pipes, 10-inch pipes and 1-inch pipes as the digits say: 1 × 100 + 3 × 10 + 7 × 1. The number of pipes is 1 + 3 + 7 = 11.

label: A3
stem: Which binary pipes (one of each length: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) add up to a height of 45 inches?
solution: Take the biggest pipe that fits each time: 45 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1. Each length is used once.

label: A4
stem: Which binary pipes (one of each length: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) add up to a height of 90 inches?
solution: Take the biggest pipe that fits each time: 90 = 64 + 16 + 8 + 2. Each length is used once.

label: A5
stem: What is the binary representation of 13?
solution: Write 13 as a sum of powers of 2: 8 + 4 + 1. Put 1 under each power used and 0 under the others: 1101.

label: A6
stem: What is the binary representation of 25?
solution: Write 25 as a sum of powers of 2: 16 + 8 + 1. Put 1 under each power used and 0 under the others: 11001.

label: A7
stem: What is the decimal value of the binary number (101101)₂?
solution: Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32: 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.

label: A8
stem: What is the decimal value of the binary number (110011)₂?
solution: Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32: 32 + 16 + 2 + 1 = 51.

label: A9
stem: How is a height of 59 inches written using ternary pipes (base 3)?
solution: Divide by 3 again and again and read the remainders upward: 59 = 2 × 27 + 1 × 3 + 2 × 1. So the ternary form is 2012.

label: A10
stem: How is a height of 85 inches written using ternary pipes (base 3)?
solution: Divide by 3 again and again and read the remainders upward: 85 = 1 × 81 + 1 × 3 + 1 × 1. So the ternary form is 10011.

label: A11
stem: Which of these cannot be a number written in base 4?
solution: Base 4 allows only the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3. The number 1234 contains the digit 4, which is not allowed.

label: A12
stem: What is the largest digit allowed in base 6?
solution: Base n uses n different digits, 0 to n − 1. For base 6 the digits are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so the largest is 5.

label: A13
stem: What is the decimal value of the ternary number (2101)₃?
solution: Place values from the right are 1, 3, 9, 27: 2 × 27 + 1 × 9 + 0 × 3 + 1 × 1 = 64.

label: A14
stem: What is the decimal value of the ternary number (1202)₃?
solution: Place values from the right are 1, 3, 9, 27: 1 × 27 + 2 × 9 + 0 × 3 + 2 × 1 = 47.

stem: Some terms are missing from this sequence written in Roman numerals. Find the missing terms, in order from left to right. XIV, VIII, XIII, IX, XII, X, _____, _____, X, XII
solution: Read the terms as numbers: 14, 8, 13, 9, 12, 10, 11, 11, 10, 12. Terms in odd places go down by 1 each time (14, 13, 12, 11, 10) and terms in even places go up by 1 (8, 9, 10, 11, 12). The missing terms are 11 and 11, that is XI, XI.

stem: Some terms are missing from this sequence written in Roman numerals. Find the missing terms, in order from left to right. XIX, IX, XVIII, X, XVII, XI, _____, _____, XV, XIII
solution: Read the terms as numbers: 19, 9, 18, 10, 17, 11, 16, 12, 15, 13. Terms in odd places go down by 1 each time (19, 18, 17, 16, 15) and terms in even places go up by 1 (9, 10, 11, 12, 13). The missing terms are 16 and 12, that is XVI, XII.

stem: How many of these comparisons are correct?
solution: XC = 90, so "XC < 89" is false; CDX = 410, so "CDX = 410" is true; MCM = 1900, so "MCM > 1899" is true; XLIX = 49, so "XLIX > 50" is false. So 2 are correct.

stem: How many of these comparisons are correct?
solution: CXL = 140, so "CXL = 140" is true; XLVII = 47, so "XLVII < 48" is true; DCCC = 800, so "DCCC = 800" is true; CMXC = 990, so "CMXC < 990" is false. So 3 are correct.

stem: An abacus with 6 poles (lakhs, ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) shows the number 3,62,046, with that many beads on each pole. Exactly one bead must be moved from one pole to a different pole (a pole can hold at most 9 beads, and the first pole must keep at least one). What is the largest possible 6- digit number now?
solution: To increase the number the most, take a bead from the ones pole and put it on the lakhs pole. This gives 4,62,045.

stem: An abacus with 6 poles (lakhs, ten-thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) shows the number 5,27,038, with that many beads on each pole. Exactly one bead must be moved from one pole to a different pole (a pole can hold at most 9 beads, and the first pole must keep at least one). What is the smallest possible 6- digit number now?
solution: To decrease the number the most, take a bead from the lakhs pole and put it on the ones pole. This gives 4,27,039.

stem: In which base is the statement 5 + 4 = 12 true?
solution: In base b, the number 12 means 1 × b + 2. Since 5 + 4 = 9, we need b + 2 = 9, so b = 7.

stem: In which base is the statement 13 × 4 = 100 true?
options: 6 In a number code, the 9 The number is the total What number is written
5 ⌒ symbol stands for 100,^◎ of its symbols. For example, ⌒⌒⌒⌒⌒⌒ ?^◎^❙❙

stem: Which option shows the number 208?
solution: The number 208 has 2 hundreds, 0 tens and 8 ones, so it needs 2 hundred-symbols, no ten-symbols, and 8 one- symbols.

stem: Two 2-digit numbers are shown with balls stacked on poles. You must move exactly one ball from one pole to any other pole (a pole holds at most 9 balls). What is the minimum possible difference between the two numbers after the move?
solution: Now the numbers are 47 and 63, a difference of 16. Trying all moves, the best is to move a ball from the tens pole of Number 2 to the tens pole of Number 1, which leaves a difference of 4.

stem: Two 2-digit numbers are shown with balls stacked on poles. You must move exactly one ball from one pole to any other pole (a pole holds at most 9 balls). What is the minimum possible difference between the two numbers after the move?
solution: Now the numbers are 58 and 26, a difference of 32. Trying all moves, the best is to move a ball from the tens pole of Number 1 to the tens pole of Number 2, which leaves a difference of 12.

stem: Sam makes a 4-digit password by pressing buttons from three screens (each button red or blue), in the order the digits appear in the password. • Each button pressed must show a greater digit than the one before • Two buttons pressed one after the other must not be on the same screen and not the same colour How many different passwords can Sam form?
solution: Check every increasing set of digits against the two rules. The passwords are: 2348, 2346, 3469. That is 3 passwords.

stem: Sam makes a 3-digit password by pressing buttons from three screens (each button red or blue), in the order the digits appear in the password. • Each button pressed must show a greater digit than the one before • Two buttons pressed one after the other must not be on the same screen and not the same colour How many different passwords can Sam form?
solution: Check every increasing set of digits against the two rules. The passwords are: 124, 125, 127, 126, 129. That is 5 passwords.

stem: Rearrange the blocks of Set A into the ascending order of Set B. Only neighbouring blocks (blocks that share a side) can be swapped. What is the minimum number of swaps? (Blocks that touch only at a corner are not neighbours.)
solution: Each swap fixes at most two blocks; trying every sequence of neighbour swaps (a shortest-path search) shows that 4 swaps are needed and fewer cannot work.

stem: Rearrange the blocks of Set A into the ascending order of Set B. Only neighbouring blocks (blocks that share a side) can be swapped. What is the minimum number of swaps? (Blocks that touch only at a corner are not neighbours.)
solution: Each swap fixes at most two blocks; trying every sequence of neighbour swaps (a shortest-path search) shows that 5 swaps are needed and fewer cannot work.

stem: Add the base-3 numbers: (212) 3 + (121) 3 . What is the sum, written in base 3?
solution: Convert to decimal: 212 = 23 and 121 = 16. The sum is 39, which in base 3 is 1110.

stem: Add the base-2 numbers: (1011) 2 + (110) 2 . What is the sum, written in base 2?
solution: Convert to decimal: 1011 = 11 and 110 = 6. The sum is 17, which in base 2 is 10001.

stem: What is the largest number (in decimal) that can be written using 5 digits in base 3?
solution: The largest 5-digit base-3 number is 22222, which is 2 × (81 + 27 + 9 + 3 + 1) = 242. It is one less than 3⁵ = 243.

stem: Binary pipes of lengths 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 inches are available, one of each. How many different whole-number heights from 1 inch upwards can be measured by choosing some of the pipes?
solution: Each pipe is either used or not: 2⁶ = 64 choices, which gives the heights 0 to 63. Leaving out 0 (no pipes), there are 63 heights.

label: P1
stem: A, B and C start at the same time from the points shown on a circular track of length 400 m (distances are measured clockwise from the top point), and all run clockwise. B runs at half the speed of A, and C runs at twice the speed of A. A starts at 50 m, B at 150 m and C at 300 m. Where are A and B when C has completed exactly one full round?
solution: C runs 400 m, so the time taken is 400 ÷ (speed of C). In that time A covers 200 m and B covers 100 m. A: 50 + 200 = 250 m (on the circle). B: 150 + 100 = 250 m.

label: P2
stem: A, B and C start at the same time from the points shown on a circular track of length 360 m (distances are measured clockwise from the top point), and all run clockwise. B runs at one-third of the speed of A, and C runs at three times the speed of A. A starts at 40 m, B at 200 m and C at 120 m. Where are A and B when C has completed exactly one full round?
solution: C runs 360 m, so the time taken is 360 ÷ (speed of C). In that time A covers 120 m and B covers 40 m. A: 40 + 120 = 160 m (on the circle). B: 200 + 40 = 240 m.

stem: Four shapes (Rhombus, Square, Trapezium, Kite) are each painted with a different colour from Red, Yellow, Green and Blue. The shape with every angle 90° is painted Red. No shape with all four sides equal is painted Green. The shape with exactly one pair of parallel sides is painted Yellow. What colour is the Rhombus?
solution: Work through the clues one at a time and cross out colours: Clue 1 places red or removes it. Clue 2 places green or removes it. Clue 3 places yellow or removes it. The only assignment that fits all three is: Rhombus – Blue, Square – Red, Trapezium – Yellow, Kite – Green.

stem: Four shapes (Rhombus, Parallelogram, Rectangle, Kite) are each painted with a different colour from Red, Yellow, Green and Blue. The shape with diagonals equal is painted Blue. No shape with both pairs of opposite sides parallel is painted Red. No shape with all four sides equal is painted Green. What colour is the Parallelogram?
solution: Work through the clues one at a time and cross out colours: Clue 1 places blue or removes it. Clue 2 places red or removes it. Clue 3 places green or removes it. The only assignment that fits all three is: Rhombus – Yellow, Parallelogram – Green, Rectangle – Blue, Kite – Red.

stem: How many rectangles (including squares) are there in this figure (of all sizes)?
solution: A rectangle is fixed by choosing 2 of the 3 horizontal lines and 2 of the 5 vertical lines: 3 × 10 = 30.

stem: How many squares are there in this figure (of all sizes)?
solution: Squares of side 1: 15. Side 2: 8. Side 3: 3. Total 15 + 8 + 3 = 26.

stem: How many quadrilaterals are there in this figure (of all sizes)?
solution: The 3 long diagonals cut the hexagon into 6 equilateral triangles. Two neighbouring triangles make a rhombus (6 of these). Three neighbouring triangles make a trapezium (6 of these). Total: 6 + 6 = 12.

stem: How many trapeziums are there in this figure (of all sizes)?
solution: Each trapezium lies between two of the 4 parallel lines (3 lines inside the triangle plus the base): 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6.

stem: How many quadrilaterals are there in this figure (of all sizes)?
solution: Rectangles: 4 small squares, 4 rectangles made of two small squares, and the whole square = 9. The other 8 shapes are trapeziums cut off by a diagonal (exactly one pair of parallel sides). Total 9 + 8 = 17.

stem: How many quadrilaterals are there in this figure (of all sizes)?
solution: Counting by type: 5 parallelograms (thin rhombus shapes), 10 trapeziums and 5 kites give 20 quadrilaterals.

stem: Look at these six shapes: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium and kite. How many of them have diagonals that bisect each other and every angle equal to 90°?
solution: In a square and a rectangle the diagonals bisect each other and all angles are 90°. In a rhombus and a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other but the angles are not always 90°. A trapezium and a kite do not have diagonals that bisect each other. So the answer is 2.

stem: Which shape always has perpendicular diagonals but its diagonals do not bisect each other?
solution: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular and bisect each other. A rectangle and a parallelogram have diagonals that bisect each other but are not always perpendicular. In a kite the diagonals are perpendicular, but only one diagonal cuts the other in half, so they do not bisect each other.

stem: Four sets of angles (in order around a quadrilateral) are given. Three of them can be the angles of a parallelogram. Which set cannot?
solution: A parallelogram has equal opposite angles, and neighbouring angles add up to 180°. In 65°, 115°, 75°, 105° the opposite angles 65° and 75° are not equal, so this set cannot belong to a parallelogram even though it adds up to 360°.

stem: One angle of a rhombus is 64°. The diagonal drawn from that corner makes what angle with each side of the rhombus?
solution: The diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angle at the corner it starts from. Half of 64° is 32°.

stem: In trapezium ABCD, AB is parallel to DC and angle A = 65°. What is angle D?
solution: AD is a slanting side between the two parallel lines, so angles A and D are co-interior angles and add up to 180°. D = 180° − 65° = 115°.

stem: Two identical equilateral triangles are joined along a full side, without overlapping. What quadrilateral is formed?
solution: All four sides of the new shape are equal to the triangle side, and its opposite angles are 60° and 120°. A shape with four equal sides and no right angle is a rhombus.

stem: Two identical right-angled triangles with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm are joined along the 5 cm side, one being the mirror image of the other. What quadrilateral is formed?
solution: Mirroring across the hypotenuse gives two sides of 3 cm next to each other and two sides of 4 cm next to each other. A shape with two pairs of equal neighbouring sides is a kite.

stem: Two identical right-angled triangles with sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm are joined along the 10 cm side, one being the mirror image of the other, to form a kite. What is the perimeter of the kite?
solution: The kite has two sides of 6 cm and two sides of 8 cm: 6 + 6 + 8 + 8 = 28 cm.

stem: Two pairs of parallel paths in a garden cross to form a parallelogram-shaped lawn. The paths are 7 m apart in one direction (side 7 m) and the other pair of sides are each 11 m long. What is the perimeter of the lawn?
solution: Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal: 7 + 11 + 7 + 11 = 36 m.

stem: The diagonals of parallelogram ABCD meet at O. AC = 18 cm, BD = 12 cm and AB = 10 cm. What is the perimeter of triangle AOB?
solution: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so AO = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 cm and BO = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm. Perimeter = 9 + 6 + 10 = 25 cm.

stem: A rectangular sheet of 13 cm × 8 cm is cut into squares as follows: cut the largest possible square from it, then cut the largest possible squares from the strip that is left, and keep going until nothing is left. How many squares are cut in all?
solution: Cut the biggest square each time: from 13×8 cut 1 square(s) of side 8; from 8×5 cut 1 square(s) of side 5; from 5×3 cut 1 square(s) of side 3; from 3×2 cut 1 square(s) of side 2; from 2×1 cut 2 square(s) of side 1. Total = 6 squares.

stem: A rectangular sheet of 17 cm × 5 cm is cut into squares as follows: cut the largest possible square from it, then cut the largest possible squares from the strip that is left, and keep going until nothing is left. How many squares are cut in all?
solution: Cut the biggest square each time: from 17×5 cut 3 square(s) of side 5; from 5×2 cut 2 square(s) of side 2; from 2×1 cut 2 square(s) of side 1. Total = 7 squares.

label: P1
stem: A 3 × 3 board has lights, shown yellow when ON and grey when OFF. Pressing a square flips that square and the squares that share a side with it (ON becomes OFF and OFF becomes ON). What is the least number of presses needed to switch every light OFF?
solution: Pressing the same square twice does nothing, so each square is pressed 0 or 1 times. Trying all 512 combinations shows that the smallest working set has 3 presses.

stem: A 3 × 3 board has lights, shown yellow when ON and grey when OFF. Pressing a square flips that square and the squares that share a side with it (ON becomes OFF and OFF becomes ON). What is the least number of presses needed to switch every light OFF?
solution: Pressing the same square twice does nothing, so each square is pressed 0 or 1 times. Trying all 512 combinations shows that the smallest working set has 3 presses.

stem: What is the largest 5-digit number with all different digits that is divisible by 12?
solution: Start from 98765 and look for numbers divisible by 12 (divisible by both 3 and 4) that have no repeated digit. Checking downwards, the first one that works is 98760.

stem: Two different 2-digit numbers are multiples of 6 but not multiples of 12. What is the smallest possible sum of the two numbers?
solution: The 2-digit multiples of 6 that are not multiples of 12 are 18, 30, 42, 54, 66, … The two smallest are 18 and 30, so the least sum is 48.

stem: There are 30 bulbs in a row, numbered 1 to 30, all switched OFF. Person 1 flips every bulb, person 2 flips every 2nd bulb, person 3 flips every 3rd bulb, and so on up to person 30. (Flipping turns ON to OFF and OFF to ON.) How many bulbs are ON at the end?
solution: Bulb number b is flipped once for each divisor of b. It ends ON only if it has an odd number of divisors, which happens only for perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25). So 5 bulbs are ON.

stem: There are 50 bulbs in a row, numbered 1 to 50, all switched OFF. Person 1 flips every bulb, person 2 flips every 2nd bulb, person 3 flips every 3rd bulb, and so on up to person 50. (Flipping turns ON to OFF and OFF to ON.) How many bulbs are ON at the end?
solution: Bulb number b is flipped once for each divisor of b. It ends ON only if it has an odd number of divisors, which happens only for perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49). So 7 bulbs are ON.

stem: The numbers 1 to 60 are written on cards. Card numbers that are multiples of 4 go in Box A, and card numbers that are multiples of 6 go in Box B (a card may go in both boxes). How many cards go in neither box?
solution: Multiples of 4: 15. Multiples of 6: 10. Multiples of both (multiples of 12): 5. Cards in at least one box: 15 + 10 − 5 = 20. Cards in neither: 60 − 20 = 40.

stem: How many numbers from 1 to 100 are multiples of 6 or 8 (or both)?
solution: Multiples of 6: 16. Multiples of 8: 12. Multiples of both (multiples of 24): 4. So 16 + 12 − 4 = 24.

stem: The numbers 23 and 38 are multiplied together. What is the remainder when the product is divided by 9?
solution: 23 leaves remainder 5 and 38 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 9. The product of the remainders is 5 × 2 = 10, which leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9.

stem: Two dice, each numbered 1 to 6, are rolled. In how many of the 36 possible outcomes is the sum of the two numbers divisible by 4?
Two dice, each numbered 1 to 6, are rolled. In how many of the 36 possible outcomes is the product of the two numbers divisible by 6?
solution: The product is a multiple of 6 if one number is 6 (11 outcomes: 6 with any number, and any number with 6, counting (6,6) once), or if the numbers are 2 and 3, or 3 and 4 in either order: (2,3), (3,2), (3,4), (4,3) = 4 outcomes. Total 11 + 4 = 15.

stem: A grandfather's age is a 2-digit number that is a multiple of both 6 and 11. How old is he?
solution: A number divisible by both 6 and 11 is a multiple of 66. The only 2-digit multiple of 66 is 66.

stem: A teacher's age is between 50 and 90 and is a multiple of both 8 and 9. How old is the teacher?
solution: A number divisible by 8 and 9 is a multiple of 72. The only multiple of 72 between 50 and 90 is 72.

stem: The sum of five consecutive even numbers is 130. What is the largest of the five numbers?
solution: The middle number is the average: 130 ÷ 5 = 26. The five numbers are 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, so the largest is 30.

stem: The sum of five consecutive odd numbers is 205. What is the smallest of the five numbers?
solution: The middle number is 205 ÷ 5 = 41. The five numbers are 37, 39, 41, 43, 45, so the smallest is 37.

stem: A 2-digit number is exactly 3 times the sum of its two digits. What is the number?
solution: Let the number be 10a + b. Then 10a + b = 3a + 3b, so 7a = 2b. The only digits that work are a = 2 and b = 7. Check: 27 = 3 × (2 + 7).

stem: How many 2-digit numbers are exactly 4 times the sum of their digits?
solution: 10a + b = 4a + 4b gives 6a = 3b, so b = 2a. The numbers are 12, 24, 36, 48, which is 4 numbers.

stem: Each of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is used once to make a 5-digit number. How many of these numbers are divisible by 4?
solution: A number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits are. From the digits 1–5 the possible endings are 12, 24, 32 and 52. Each ending leaves 3 digits to arrange in 3! = 6 ways, so 4 × 6 = 24.

stem: How many 3-digit numbers with three different digits from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are divisible by 5?
solution: The last digit must be 5. The first two digits are chosen from the other 5 digits in 5 × 4 = 20 ways.

stem: What is the largest 4-digit number with all different digits that is divisible by 8?
solution: Check numbers downwards from 9876. A number is divisible by 8 if its last three digits are. The largest one with no repeated digit is 9872.

stem: What is the smallest number greater than 1 that leaves remainder 1 when divided by each of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6?
solution: The number is one more than a common multiple of 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. The smallest common multiple is 60, so the number is 60 + 1 = 61.

stem: How many 2-digit numbers are there such that the number minus the number formed by reversing its digits is exactly 27? (Example: 52 − 25 = 27.)
solution: For digits a and b, (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9(a − b). We need 9(a − b) = 27, so a − b = 3. The numbers are 30, 41, 52, 63, 74, 85 and 96, which is 7 numbers.

label: P1
stem: Twelve lamps are in a row, numbered 1 to 12, all OFF. In round 1 every lamp is flipped, in round 2 every 2nd lamp, in round 3 every 3rd lamp, and so on up to round 12. How many lamps are ON at the end?
solution: A lamp is flipped once for each of its divisors, so it is ON only when it has an odd number of divisors, that is, when its number is a perfect square: lamps 1, 4 and 9. So 3 lamps are ON.

label: P2
stem: Thirty lamps are numbered 1 to 30, all OFF. In round 1 every 2nd lamp is flipped (2, 4, 6, …). In round 2 every 3rd lamp is flipped (3, 6, 9, …). How many lamps are ON at the end?
solution: Lamps that are multiples of 2: 15. Multiples of 3: 10. Multiples of both (6): 5. A lamp is ON if it was flipped exactly once, so it is a multiple of 2 or 3 but not of 6: 15 + 10 − 2 × 5 = 15.

stem: A secret code is calculated as (a + b)(c + d) − (a − b)(c − d). What is the code when a = 3, b = 4, c = 5 and d = 2?
A secret code is calculated as (a + b)(c + d) − (a − b)(c − d). What is the code when a = 5, b = 2, c = 6 and d = 3?
Use (x − y)(x + y) = x² − y² to find 47 × 53 quickly. What is the product?
What is 998 × 1002? (Think of both numbers as being the same distance from 1000.)
What is 105 × 95? (Think of both numbers as being the same distance from 100.)
A square garden has side 15 m. Its length is increased by 3 m and its width is decreased by 3 m, giving a rectangular garden. What is the area of the new garden?
solution: New area = (15 + 3)(15 − 3) = 15² − 3² = 225 − 9 = 216 square metres. It is 9 m² less than the original.

stem: A shop packs coins in bags. There are 3 bags with (x + 4) coins each and 2 bags with (x − 1) coins each. How many coins are there in all when x = 10?
solution: Bags of the first kind: 3 × (10 + 4) = 42. Bags of the second kind: 2 × (9) = 18. Total = 60.

stem: A shop packs coins in bags. There are 4 bags with (x + 3) coins each and 3 bags with (2x − 1) coins each. How many coins are there in all when x = 7?
solution: Bags of the first kind: 4 × (7 + 3) = 40. Bags of the second kind: 3 × (13) = 39. Total = 79.

stem: A 2-digit number is added to the number formed by reversing its digits, and the sum is 143. What is the sum of the two digits?
solution: For digits a and b, (10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11(a + b). So 11(a + b) = 143 and a + b = 143 ÷ 11 = 13.

stem: How many 2-digit numbers have the property that the number minus its reversal is exactly 63?
solution: For digits a and b, (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9(a − b). So 9(a − b) = 63 and a − b = 7. The numbers are 70, 81, 92, which is 3 numbers.

stem: The digit in the hundreds place of the number 47□21 is missing, written as □. For how many choices of this digit (0 to 9) is the number divisible by 3?
solution: A number is divisible by 3 when its digit sum is. The known digits add to 4 + 7 + 2 + 1 = 14, so □ must make 14 + □ a multiple of 3: □ = 1, 4, 7, which is 3 choices.

stem: A painter paints (n + 2) walls a day for 5 days, and then (n − 1) walls a day for 4 days. How many walls does the painter paint in all when n = 6?
solution: First part: 5 × (6 + 2) = 40. Second part: 4 × (6 − 1) = 20. Total = 60. As an expression: 9n + 6.

stem: A family buys 2 adult and 3 child tickets for the journey there, and 1 adult and 1 child ticket for the journey back. An adult ticket costs ₹120 and a child ticket costs ₹70. What is the total cost?
solution: Adult tickets: 2 + 1 = 3, costing 3 × 120 = 360. Child tickets: 3 + 1 = 4, costing 4 × 70 = 280. Total = 360 + 280 = 640.

stem: Which expression is equal to 6(x + 2) − 2(x − 3) for every value of x?
solution: 6(x + 2) = 6x + 12 and 2(x − 3) = 2x − 6. Subtracting: 6x + 12 − 2x + 6 = 4x + 18. (Careful: subtracting −6 adds 6.)

stem: Which expression is equal to (x + 3)(x + 4) for every value of x?
solution: Multiply each term: x × x = x², x × 4 = 4x, 3 × x = 3x, 3 × 4 = 12. Adding: x² + 4x + 3x + 12 = x² + 7x + 12.

stem: What is the value of (x + 5)(x − 5) when x = 12?
If a + b = 10 and ab = 21, what is the value of a² + b²?
solution: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², so a² + b² = (a + b)² − 2ab = 100 − 42 = 58.

stem: If a − b = 4 and ab = 12, what is the value of a² + b²?
solution: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², so a² + b² = (a − b)² + 2ab = 16 + 24 = 40.

stem: 7 mangoes and 3 apples cost ₹140. 3 mangoes and 7 apples cost ₹100. What is the cost of 5 mangoes and 5 apples?
solution: Add the two bills: 10 mangoes and 10 apples cost 140 + 100 = ₹240. Half of that is 5 mangoes and 5 apples: ₹120.

stem: Notice the pattern: 1 × 3 + 1 = 2², 2 × 4 + 1 = 3², 3 × 5 + 1 = 4². What is 49 × 51 + 1?
solution: n(n + 2) + 1 = n² + 2n + 1 = (n + 1)². Here n = 49, so the answer is 50² = 2500.

label: P1
stem: Two coins are hidden in different cells of a 4 × 4 grid. The two coins must not be in the same row and not in the same column. In how many different ways can the coins be hidden? (The coins are identical.)
solution: Choose any cell for the first coin (16 ways). The second coin must avoid its row and column, leaving 9 cells. That counts each pair twice: 16 × 9 ÷ 2 = 72.

label: P2
stem: Two identical coins are hidden in different cells of a 4 × 4 grid. The two coins must not touch: they cannot share a side or even a corner. In how many different ways can the coins be hidden?
solution: Total pairs of cells: 16 × 15 ÷ 2 = 120. Touching pairs: 12 side-by-side, 12 one-above-the-other and 18 diagonal = 42. So 120 − 42 = 78 ways.

stem: A fruit basket has apples and oranges in the ratio 3 : 5. There are 40 fruits in all. How many oranges are there?
solution: The ratio has 3 + 5 = 8 parts. One part is 40 ÷ 8 = 5 fruits. Oranges are 5 parts: 5 × 5 = 25.

stem: A bag has red and blue marbles in the ratio 3 : 4. When 6 more red marbles are added, the number of red marbles becomes equal to the number of blue marbles. How many marbles were in the bag at the start?
solution: Red = 3k and blue = 4k. Adding 6 red gives 3k + 6 = 4k, so k = 6. The bag started with 3 × 6 + 4 × 6 = 42 marbles.

stem: Two 2-digit numbers are in the ratio 2 : 3, and both numbers have two different digits. How many such pairs of numbers are there? (Example: 14 and 21 is not allowed because the ratio is not 2 : 3. 20 : 30 is allowed.)
solution: The numbers are 2k and 3k with both having 2 digits, so k runs from 5 to 33. Checking each k and removing pairs where a number repeats a digit (like 22, 33, 44, 66, 99) leaves 26 pairs.

stem: A 40-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 2. How many litres of water must be added so that the ratio of milk to water becomes 1 : 1?
solution: Milk = 40 × 3/5 = 24 litres and water = 16 litres. For a 1 : 1 ratio the water must also be 24 litres, so add 24 − 16 = 8 litres.

stem: ₹2000 is shared among three children in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. How much does the child with the largest share get?
solution: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts, so one part is 2000 ÷ 10 = ₹200. The largest share is 5 parts: 5 × 200 = ₹1000.

stem: The ages of three sisters are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4 and add up to 72 years. How old is the eldest sister?
solution: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts, so one part is 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years. The eldest has 4 parts: 4 × 8 = 32 years.

stem: Asha and Ben share their pocket money in the ratio 3 : 5. Ben gets ₹200 more than Asha. How much does Asha get?
solution: Ben has 5 − 3 = 2 more parts than Asha. 2 parts = ₹200, so 1 part = ₹100. Asha gets 3 parts = ₹300.

stem: A 12-hour digital clock shows times from 1:00 to 12:59. At how many of these times is the hour : minutes ratio equal to 1 : 5? (For example, 3:15 has hour : minutes = 3 :
solution: The minutes must be 5 times the hour, and less than 60. The times are 1:05, 2:10, 3:15, 4:20, 5:25, 6:30, …. That is 11 times.

stem: A 12-hour digital clock shows times from 1:00 to 12:59. At how many of these times is the hour : minutes ratio equal to 1 : 2? (For example, 3:15 has hour : minutes = 3 :
solution: The minutes must be 2 times the hour, and less than 60. The times are 1:02, 2:04, 3:06, 4:08, 5:10, 6:12, …. That is 12 times.

stem: A shopkeeper packs apples in boxes of 12 and boxes of 8. She needs to pack exactly 100 apples using the fewest boxes. How many boxes does she use?
solution: Using x boxes of 12 and y boxes of 8: 12x + 8y = 100, so 3x + 2y = 25. The solutions are (1, 11), (3, 8), (5, 5) and (7, 2). The fewest boxes is 7 + 2 = 9.

stem: Four packs of rice are on sale: A is 250 g for ₹60, B is 400 g for ₹92, C is 150 g for ₹36 and D is 500 g for ₹120. Which pack is the cheapest per 100 g?
A car travels 150 km in 2.5 hours at a steady speed. How long will it take to travel 270 km at the same speed?
solution: Speed = 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km per hour. Time = 270 ÷ 60 = 4.5 hours.

stem: On a map, 1 cm stands for 5 km. Two towns are 7.5 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
solution: Each cm on the map is 5 km, so 7.5 cm is 7.5 × 5 = 37.5 km.

stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour to make 12 cookies. How many cups of flour are needed for 20 cookies?
solution: Flour per cookie = 3 ÷ 12 = 1/4 cup. For 20 cookies: 20 × 1/4 = 5 cups.

stem: 6 workers can finish a job in 10 days. How many days would 4 workers take to finish the same job, working at the same speed?
solution: The job needs 6 × 10 = 60 worker-days. With 4 workers: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 days.

stem: The sides of a rectangle are in the ratio 3 : 2 and its perimeter is 50 cm. What is its area?
solution: The perimeter is 2 × (3 parts + 2 parts) = 10 parts = 50 cm, so one part is 5 cm. The sides are 15 cm and 10 cm, and the area is 15 × 10 = 150 cm².

stem: A row of 60 shapes has stars and circles in the ratio 3 : 2. How many stars are there?
solution: 3 + 2 = 5 parts, so one part is 60 ÷ 5 = 12. Stars are 3 parts: 36.

stem: What is the ratio of 45 minutes to 2 hours in its simplest form?
solution: Write both in minutes: 2 hours = 120 minutes. 45 : 120 = 3 : 8 after dividing both by 15.

stem: A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5. If A = 16, what is C?
solution: Make B the same in both ratios: A : B = 8 : 12 and B : C = 12 : 15, so A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15. A = 16 is 2 × 8, so C = 2 × 15 = 30.

stem: A father is 40 years old and his son is 10 years old. In how many years will the father's age be exactly 3 times the son's age?
solution: After x years: 40 + x = 3(10 + x) = 30 + 3x, so 10 = 2x and x = 5. Check: 45 = 3 × 15.

label: P1
stem: A tank can be filled by pipe A alone in 6 hours and by pipe B alone in 3 hours. If both pipes are opened together, how many hours will they take to fill the empty tank?
solution: Pipe A fills 1/6 of the tank each hour and pipe B fills 1/3. Together they fill 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 each hour, so the tank is full in 2 hours.

label: P2
stem: A tank is filled by pipe A in 10 minutes. A second pipe C can empty the full tank in 15 minutes. If both are opened together on an empty tank, how many minutes will it take to fill?
solution: Pipe A adds 1/10 of the tank per minute and pipe C removes 1/15 per minute. The net gain is 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30 per minute, so it takes 30 minutes.
